From these graphs, we derive zero-shot language-based tasks spanning phrase grounding, hand-object interaction recognition, referring, activity recognition, relation extraction, and temporal visual question answering. Experiments reveal strong variation across task families and no consistently dominant model family, positioning BARISTA as a challenging diagnostic benchmark for procedural video understanding. Code and dataset available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Attention Sinks in Diffusion Transformers: A Causal Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09313)**  `arXiv:2605.09313`  
  _Fangzheng Wu, Brian Summa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Attention sinks -- tokens that receive disproportionate attention mass -- are assumed to be functionally important in autoregressive language models, but their role in diffusion transformers remains unclear. We present a causal analysis in text-to-image diffusion, dynamically identifying dominant attention recipients per timestep and suppressing them via paired, training-free interventions on the score and value paths. Across 553 GenEval prompts on Stable Diffusion~3 (with SDXL corroboration), removing these sinks does not degrade text-image alignment (CLIP-T) or preference proxies (ImageReward, HPS-v2) at $k{=}1$; only under stronger interventions ($k\!\geq\!10$) does HPS-v2 exhibit a metric-dependent boundary, while CLIP-T remains robust throughout. The perceptual shifts induced by suppression are nonetheless \emph{sink-specific} -- $\sim\!6\times$ larger than equal-budget random masking -- revealing an empirical dissociation between trajectory-level perturbation and \emph{semantic alignment} in diffusion transformers. \footnote{Code available atthis https URL.}
  </details>

- **[Can MLLMs Reason About Visual Persuasion? Evaluating the Efficacy and Faithfulness of Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08965)**  `arXiv:2605.08965`  
  _Naeun Lee, Hyunjong Kim, Sunghwan Choi, Injin Kong, Yohan Jo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Persuasive visuals play a central role in advertising, public communication, and online media, making it increasingly important to understand whether an image is persuasive and why. However, current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have limited ability to reason about visual persuasion. Our analysis reveals that models often rely on a shortcut---selectively citing easily recognizable visual elements and treating their mere presence as evidence of persuasiveness---rather than reasoning over the diverse visual cues in an image to determine how and why they contribute to persuasiveness. To address this limitation, we propose (1) a fine-tuning approach that trains models on rationales reflecting diverse perspectives on visual persuasiveness, and (2) an evaluation framework that measures the faithfulness of models' rationales through three complementary metrics. Fine-tuning on multi-perspective rationales improves persuasiveness prediction and reasoning effectiveness. However, our evaluation framework reveals a discrepancy between prediction performance and rationale faithfulness, showing that higher prediction performance does not necessarily correspond to more faithful reasoning. These findings highlight the need to evaluate effectiveness and faithfulness separately and inform future directions for improving both the training and evaluation of visual persuasion reasoning.
  </details>

- **[ProSG: Learning Progressive Structural Guidance for 3D Human Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08806)**  `arXiv:2605.08806`  
  _Zehua Wang, Qiongjie Cui, Changwang Mei, Huaijiang Sun, Pengqi Hu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  For 3D human pose estimation from detected 2D joint locations, depth ambiguity remains a fundamental challenge. Even when two connected joints are accurately localized in the image, their relative depth along the camera axis can remain uncertain. Existing methods progressively refine pose representations through successive stages, with early stages emphasizing local 2D skeletal geometry and joint relationships and deeper stages developing increasingly depth-related representations. However, early-stage structural cues remain overlooked despite their importance for subsequent 3D inference. Our findings reveal that reusing such information provides complementary geometric guidance, particularly improving joint position estimation along the camera-space depth axis. We propose ProSG, a progressive structural guidance framework that preserves and aggregates intermediate pose representations from preceding stages to guide subsequent 3D pose refinement. Specifically, Structure Guided Accumulation (SGA) maintains a pool of these representations and adaptively retrieves relevant information for each joint and frame, enabling deeper stages to revisit early structural cues. Structural Context Reorganization (SCR) further reorganizes intermediate representations before they enter the representation pool, using compact structural contextual tokens to facilitate the effective integration of structural information across stages. Extensive experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP demonstrate the effectiveness of ProSG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
  </details>

- **[Text-to-CAD Evaluation with CADTests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07807)**  `arXiv:2605.07807`  
  _Dimitrios Mallis, Marco Wang, Ahmet Serdar Karadeniz, Elisa Ricci, Anis Kacem, Djamila Aouada_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Text-to-CAD has recently emerged as an important task with the potential to substantially accelerate design workflows. Despite its significance, there has been surprisingly little work on Text-to-CAD evaluation, and assessing CAD model generation performance remains a considerable challenge. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation perspective for Text-to-CAD based on automated testing. We propose CADTestBench, the first test-based benchmark for Text-to-CAD, based on CADTests, executable software tests that verify whether a generated CAD model satisfies the geometric and topological requirements of the input prompt. Using CADTestBench, we conduct comprehensive benchmarking of recent Text-to-CAD methods and further demonstrate that CADTests can also guide CAD model generation, yielding simple baselines that surpass performance of current methods. CADTestBench code and data are available.
  </details>

- **[SIEVES: Selective Prediction Generalizes through Visual Evidence Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25855)**  `arXiv:2604.25855`  
  _Hector G. Rodriguez, Marcus Rohrbach_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As the accuracy of Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on traditional visual question answering benchmarks approaches saturation, reliable deployment requires satisfying low error tolerances in real-world out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Selective prediction aims to improve coverage, i.e. the share of inputs the system answers, while adhering to a user-defined risk level. This is typically achieved by assigning a confidence score to each answer and abstaining on those that fall below a certain threshold. Existing selective prediction methods rely on text-only reasoning and learn to predict confidences simply based on whether the answer was correct or not. In contrast, we introduce SIEVES (Selective Prediction through Visual Evidence Scoring), which first requires the answering model to provide visual evidence supporting its answer, by returning crops of the image alongside their textual reasoning and answer. Second, a lightweight selector is trained to predict the quality of this evidence, assessing how well the provided crops localize the relevant visual elements and if the final answer is coherent with this evidence. We show that SIEVES improves coverage by up to six times on challenging OOD benchmarks (V* Bench, HR-Bench-8k, MME-RealWorld-Lite, VizWiz, and AdVQA), compared to non-grounding baselines. Beyond better generalization to OOD tasks, the design of the SIEVES selector enables transfer to proprietary reasoners without access to their weights or logits, such as o3 and Gemini-3-Pro, providing coverage boosts beyond those attributable to accuracy alone. We highlight that SIEVES generalizes across all tested OOD datasets and reasoner models, without benchmark- or reasoner-specific training or adaptation.
  </details>

- **[From Clinical Intent to Clinical Model: Autonomous Coding-Agents for Clinician-driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17110)**  `arXiv:2604.17110`  
  _Zihao Zhao, Eneko Cornejo Merodio, Wenya Zhao, Frederik Hauke, Wensa Peng, Xixi Song, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  BACKGROUND: Developing clinically useful AI requires collaboration between clinicians and AI developers, yet this process often involves time-consuming communication and potential misalignment. Coding agents may help bridge this gap.METHODS: We present a prototype that lets clinicians drive AI development directly via natural-language interactions. The system turns a clinician request into an executable workflow through semantic parsing, task initialization, and iterative code tuning, using Claude Opus 4.6 as the underlying coding agent. We evaluated this prototype across 12 tasks, including straightforward requests focused solely on model performance metrics and more complex requests. The test set was held out from the beginning and was never exposed to the coding agent. An exploratory human evaluation was conducted with six clinicians who completed a questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale after interacting with the system.RESULTS: Across 12 tasks, the prototype autonomously developed AI models with competitive performance. Notably, clinicians' practical knowledge helped reduce shortcut reliance (partial correlation from 0.53 to 0.07) in pneumothorax classification. Drain-free AUROC improved in every cohort and the clinician-driven model achieved stronger lesion localization than medical foundation models across all five external cohorts. All six participants commented communication as efficient and agreed that the agent understood their clinical goals and can provide useful suggestions, but also saying extensive external testing is needed before clinical use of autonomously developed AI models.CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that coding agents could let clinicians take a more independent and active role in clinical AI development, reducing their reliance on AI developers, although further improvements are needed.
  </details>

- **[Free Geometry: Refining 3D Reconstruction from Stronger Versions of Itself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14048)**  `arXiv:2604.14048`  
  _Yuhang Dai, Xingyi Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models are efficient but rigid: once trained, they run zero-shot and cannot adapt to the test scene. As a result, plausible-looking reconstructions often contain errors under domain shifts, occlusions, specularities and ambiguous cues. To address this, we introduce Free Geometry, a framework that enables feed-forward 3D reconstruction models to self-evolve at test time without any 3D ground truth or offline retraining. Our key insight is that a model can become its own teacher at test time. When given more views, the model produces more geometrically consistent reconstructions. Aggregating multiple such predictions across different reference frames and view subsets further improves their accuracy and reliability, forming a stronger consensus teacher. Leveraging this property, given a test sequence, we mask different subsets of it to construct multiple partial observations. Free Geometry then adapts the model by enforcing camera pose and depth consistency between these partial-view predictions and the teacher's consensus. By updating only the normalization layers, this self-supervision enables fast scene-specific adaptation in about two minutes on a single GPU. Our approach improves five state-of-the-art foundation models on four datasets, yielding average relative gains of 8.8% in camera pose accuracy (AUC@3) and 3.9% in point map accuracy (inlier ratio). Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Leveraging Gaze and Set-of-Mark in VLLMs for Human-Object Interaction Anticipation from Egocentric Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03667)**  `arXiv:2604.03667`  
  _Daniele Materia, Francesco Ragusa, Giovanni Maria Farinella_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The ability to anticipate human-object interactions is highly desirable in an intelligent assistive system in order to guide users during daily life activities and understand their short and long-term goals. Creating systems with such capabilities requires to approach several complex challenges. This work addresses the problem of human-object interaction anticipation in Egocentric Vision using Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs). We tackle key limitations in existing approaches by improving visual grounding capabilities through Set-of-Mark prompting and understanding user intent via the trajectory formed by the user's most recent gaze fixations. To effectively capture the temporal dynamics immediately preceding the interaction, we further introduce a novel inverse exponential sampling strategy for input video frames. Experiments conducted on the egocentric dataset HD-EPIC demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches for the considered task, showing its model-agnostic nature.
  </details>

- **[Think, Act, Build: An Agentic Framework with Vision Language Models for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00528)**  `arXiv:2604.00528`  
  _Haibo Wang, Zihao Lin, Zhiyang Xu, Lifu Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  3D Visual Grounding (3D-VG) aims to localize objects in 3D scenes via natural language descriptions. While recent advancements leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored zero-shot possibilities, they typically suffer from a static workflow relying on preprocessed 3D point clouds, essentially degrading grounding into proposal matching. To bypass this reliance, our core motivation is to decouple the task: leveraging 2D VLMs to resolve complex spatial semantics, while relying on deterministic multi-view geometry to instantiate the 3D structure. Driven by this insight, we propose "Think, Act, Build (TAB)", a dynamic agentic framework that reformulates 3D-VG tasks as a generative 2D-to-3D reconstruction paradigm operating directly on raw RGB-D streams. Specifically, guided by a specialized 3D-VG skill, our VLM agent dynamically invokes visual tools to track and reconstruct the target across 2D frames. Crucially, to overcome the multi-view coverage deficit caused by strict VLM semantic tracking, we introduce the Semantic-Anchored Geometric Expansion, a mechanism that first anchors the target in a reference video clip and then leverages multi-view geometry to propagate its spatial location across unobserved frames. This enables the agent to "Build" the target's 3D representation by aggregating these multi-view features via camera parameters, directly mapping 2D visual cues to 3D coordinates. Furthermore, to ensure rigorous assessment, we identify flaws such as reference ambiguity and category errors in existing benchmarks and manually refine the incorrect queries. Extensive experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D demonstrate that our framework, relying entirely on open-source models, significantly outperforms previous zero-shot methods and even surpasses fully supervised baselines.
  </details>

- **[AdapTS: Lightweight Teacher-Student Approach for Multi-Class and Continual Visual Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17530)**  `arXiv:2603.17530`  
  _Manuel Barusco, Davide Dalle Pezze, Francesco Borsatti, Gian Antonio Susto_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual Anomaly Detection (VAD) is crucial for industrial inspection. However, most methods are designed for single-category models, and Teacher-Student (TS) approaches, despite their efficiency, have not been designed for the Continual scenario, where they need a replay buffer. To bridge this gap, we propose AdapTS, a unified TS framework for multi-class and continual settings, optimized for resource-constrained deployment. A single shared frozen backbone acts as teacher and student, and lightweight trainable adapters, selected at inference by a prototype-based task identification (99% accuracy), store the knowledge of each category without keeping past data. Training is enhanced via a segmentation-guided objective on synthetic Perlin noise. On MVTec AD, AdapTS-M improves I-ROC by 11 points over STFPM and needs 4.3 times less memory than Dinomaly, which is 4 points ahead. In the Continual scenario, AdapTS-M reaches the best pixel-level AP with only 0.1% forgetting and no replay buffer. AdapTS-S needs only 23 MB, and with a MobileNetV2 backbone AdapTS needs 6-7 MB while outperforming the edge-oriented STFPM on all metrics. AdapTS is thus a viable solution for resource-constrained deployment.
  </details>

- **[Towards Explainable Industrial Anomaly Detection via Knowledge-Guided Latent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09850)**  `arXiv:2602.09850`  
  _Peng Chen, Wenqiang Wang, Yunkang Cao, Chengliang Liu, Wei Wang, Mingbo Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Industrial anomaly detection demands precise reasoning over fine-grained defect patterns. However, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), pretrained on general-domain data, often struggle to capture category-specific anomalies, thereby limiting both detection accuracy and interpretability. To address these limitations, we propose Reason-IAD, a knowledge-guided dynamic latent reasoning framework for explainable industrial anomaly detection. Reason-IAD comprises two core components. First, a retrieval-augmented knowledge module incorporates category-specific textual descriptions into the model input, enabling context-aware reasoning over domain-specific defects. Second, an entropy-driven latent reasoning mechanism conducts iterative exploration within a compact latent space using optimizable latent think tokens, guided by an entropy-based reward that encourages confident and stable predictions. Furthermore, a dynamic visual injection strategy selectively incorporates the most informative image patches into the latent sequence, directing the reasoning process toward regions critical for anomaly detection. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Reason-IAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple tasks. The code will be publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[GeoFocus: Blending Efficient Global-to-Local Perception for Multimodal Geometry Problem-Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08524)**  `arXiv:2602.08524`  
  _Linger Deng, Yuliang Liu, Wenwen Yu, Zujia Zhang, Pei Fu, Zhenbo Luo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Geometry problem-solving (GPS) remains challenging for large multimodal models, partly due to limitations in geometric perception. Existing perception-oriented approaches face two key limitations: code-based diagram reconstruction relies on verbose training targets, while perception question-answering supervision may overlook local geometric relations critical to reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose GeoFocus, a global-to-local perception training framework with two complementary components. VertexLang provides compact supervision of global diagram topology through vertex coordinates and connectivity, reducing annotation length by 88% and training time by 20% compared with code-based reconstruction. The Critical Local Perceptor generates targeted question-answer supervision across 13 categories of reasoning-relevant local geometric relations. On three GPS benchmarks, GeoFocus improves Qwen3-VL-2B/4B over matched GRPO-only baselines by 5.2/4.9 percentage points on average, without external tools or additional inference steps. A human evaluation of 200 problems further shows that GeoFocus reduces cases with geometric perception errors from 118 to 80. These results highlight perception-focused training as an effective complement to reasoning optimization for multimodal geometric problem-solving.
  </details>

- **[SparVAR: Exploring Sparsity in Visual AutoRegressive Modeling for Training-Free Acceleration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04361)**  `arXiv:2602.04361`  
  _Zekun Li, Ning Wang, Tongxin Bai, Changwang Mei, Peisong Wang, Shuang Qiu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) modeling has garnered significant attention for its innovative next-scale prediction paradigm. However, mainstream VAR paradigms attend to all tokens across historical scales at each autoregressive step. As the next scale resolution grows, the computational complexity of attention increases quartically with resolution, causing substantial latency. Prior accelerations often skip high-resolution scales, which speeds up inference but discards high-frequency details and harms image quality. To address these problems, we present SparVAR, a training-free acceleration framework that exploits three properties of VAR attention: (i) strong attention sinks, (ii) cross-scale activation similarity, and (iii) pronounced locality. Specifically, we dynamically predict the sparse attention pattern of later high-resolution scales from a sparse decision scale, and construct scale self-similar sparse attention via an efficient index-mapping mechanism, enabling high-efficiency sparse attention computation at large scales. Furthermore, we propose cross-scale local sparse attention and implement an efficient block-wise sparse kernel, which achieves $\mathbf{> 5\times}$ faster forward speed than FlashAttention. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SparVAR can reduce the generation time of an 8B model producing $1024\times1024$ high-resolution images to the 1s, without skipping the last scales. Compared with the VAR baseline accelerated by FlashAttention, our method achieves a $\mathbf{1.57\times}$ speed-up while preserving almost all high-frequency details. When combined with existing scale-skipping strategies, SparVAR attains up to a $\mathbf{2.28\times}$ acceleration, while maintaining competitive visual generation quality. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Self-Supervised Uncalibrated Multi-View Video Anonymization in the Operating Room](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02850)**  `arXiv:2602.02850`  
  _Keqi Chen, Vinkle Srivastav, Armine Vardazaryan, Cindy Rolland, Didier Mutter, Nicolas Padoy_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Privacy preservation is a prerequisite for using video data in Operating Room (OR) research. Effective anonymization relies on the exhaustive localization of every individual; even a single missed detection necessitates extensive manual correction. However, existing approaches face two critical scalability bottlenecks: (1) they usually require manual annotations of each new clinical site for high accuracy; (2) while multi-camera setups have been widely adopted to address single-view ambiguity, camera calibration is typically required whenever cameras are repositioned. To address these problems, we propose a self-supervised multi-view video anonymization framework consisting of whole-body person detection and whole-body pose estimation, without annotation or camera calibration. Our core strategy is to enhance the single-view detector by "retrieving" false negatives using temporal and multi-view context, and conducting self-supervised domain adaptation. We first run an off-the-shelf whole-body person detector in each view with a low-score threshold to gather candidate detections. Then, we retrieve the low-score false negatives that exhibit consistency with the high-score detections via tracking and self-supervised uncalibrated multi-view association. These recovered detections serve as pseudo labels to iteratively fine-tune the whole-body detector. Finally, we apply whole-body pose estimation on each detected person, and fine-tune the pose model using its own high-score predictions. Experiments on the 4D-OR dataset of simulated surgeries and our dataset of real surgeries show the effectiveness of our approach achieving 99% and 97% recall, respectively. Moreover, we train a real-time whole-body detector using our pseudo labels, achieving comparable performance and highlighting our method's practical applicability. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Towards progressive whole-slide image analysis with multi-scale pyramidal network, a pathologist inspired approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01951)**  `arXiv:2602.01951`  
  _Shuyang Wu, Yifu Qiu, John-Melle Bokhorst, Ines P Nearchou, Sandrine Prost, Jonathan A Fallowfield, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Pathologists make a low power assessment followed by limited but targeted higher power evaluation of regions of interest as the standard approach in gold-standard clinical histopathological reporting. Multiple-instance Learning (MIL) is commonly used for slide-level predictions in computational pathology and approaches using multi-scale features have been developed. However, existing multi-scale MIL methods typically rely on inflexible multi-magnification inputs and computationally expensive architectures. We therefore conceptualise a more efficient MIL method that is explicitly designed to mimic the efficient gold-standard human pathologist approach to multi-scale assessment. In this paper, we propose the Multi-scale Pyramidal Network (MSPN), a generalisable module for attention-based MIL. MSPN introduces progressive multi-scale whole-slide image analysis using only a single high-magnification input. It consists of (1) grid-based remapping that aggregates high-magnification features to derive spatially-aware coarse feature maps, and (2) the Coarse Guidance Network (CGN) that learns coarse contexts. We take MSPN as a generalisable module to 4 attention-based frameworks and benchmark on 11 clinically relevant tasks across 10 publicly available datasets with 2 foundation models. Our results demonstrate that by modelling the human pathologist paradigm in slide evaluation, MSPN consistently improves MIL across the compared configurations and is competitive on performance against 8 state-of-the-art multi-scale models while remaining lightweight and accessible in a manner that may increase implementability into under-resourced clinical systems.
  </details>

- **[PLANING: A Loosely Coupled Triangle-Gaussian Framework for Streaming 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22046)**  `arXiv:2601.22046`  
  _Changjian Jiang, Kerui Ren, Xudong Li, Kaiwen Song, Guanghao Li, Linning Xu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Streaming reconstruction from monocular image sequences remains challenging, as existing methods typically favor either high-quality rendering or accurate geometry, but rarely both. We present PLANING, an efficient on-the-fly reconstruction framework built on a hybrid representation that loosely couples explicit geometric primitives with neural Gaussians, enabling geometry and appearance to be modeled in a decoupled manner. This decoupling supports an online initialization and optimization strategy that separates geometry and appearance updates, yielding stable streaming reconstruction with substantially reduced structural redundancy. Despite operating online, PLANING improves dense mesh Chamfer-L2 by 18.52% over the offline baseline PGSR, surpasses the streaming baseline ARTDECO by 1.31 dB in PSNR on average across the six evaluated datasets, and reconstructs ScanNetV2 scenes in 2.1 minutes, over 5x faster than offline 2D Gaussian Splatting while matching per-scene optimization quality. Beyond reconstruction quality, the structural clarity and computational efficiency of PLANING make it well suited for a broad range of downstream applications, such as enabling large-scale scene modeling and simulation-ready environments for embodied AI. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Where is the multimodal goal post? On the Ability of Foundation Models to Recognize Highlights in Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16333)**  `arXiv:2601.16333`  
  _Aditya K Surikuchi, Raquel Fernández, Sandro Pezzelle_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Foundation models are used for many real-world applications involving language understanding and generation from temporally-ordered multimodal events. In this work, we study the ability of models to identify the most important sub-events in a video, which is a fundamental prerequisite for summarizing, reasoning over, or narrating multimodal events. Specifically, we focus on football games and evaluate models on their ability to distinguish between important and non-important sub-events in a game. To this end, we construct a new dataset by leveraging publicly available football highlight reels containing the most important moments of a game according to professional experts, without any additional annotation costs. Using our dataset, we compare several state-of-the-art multimodal models and show that they fail to reliably capture contextual importance. Analyses of models beyond standard evaluation metrics reveal their tendency to rely on a single dominant modality and their ineffectiveness in synthesizing necessary information from multiple sources. Our findings underline the importance of modular architectures that dynamically adapt to multimodal heterogeneity and the need for complementary training procedures that maximize cross-modal synergy.
  </details>

- **[On the Role of Rotation Equivariance in Monocular 2D-to-3D Human Pose Lifting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13913)**  `arXiv:2601.13913`  
  _Pavlo Melnyk, Cuong Le, Urs Waldmann, Per-Erik Forssén, Bastian Wandt_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We consider monocular 3D human pose estimation (HPE), focusing on lifting detected 2D keypoints to 3D skeletal joints. Despite their success, we find that commonly used lifting models, including a state-of-the-art probabilistic method, exhibit substantial performance degradation under in-plane rotations. We systematically study SO(2) rotation equivariance and robustness across lifting models, comparing approaches that learn approximate equivariance via data augmentation with those that enforce exact equivariance via architectural constraints or pose canonicalisation. We investigate their effects on prediction accuracy, rotational robustness, cross-dataset generalisation, and computational efficiency. Using established HPE benchmarks, we show that rotation-based augmentation applied jointly to input and output poses substantially improves accuracy on rotated poses, reducing error by up to 72\% with little loss of original-pose accuracy. These improvements also extend to probabilistic lifting and real-world sequences containing natural full-body rotations. While augmented models can outperform specialised equivariant architectures at considerably lower inference cost, comparisons using canonicalisation-based versions of the same lifting models demonstrate that exact equivariance need not compromise prediction accuracy. Direct equivariance diagnostics further show that rotational robustness does not imply exact equivariance. Overall, the relative benefits of learning or enforcing equivariance depend on the lifting backbone and the mechanism used to achieve it.
  </details>

- **[Taming Hallucinations: Boosting MLLMs' Video Understanding via Counterfactual Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24271)**  `arXiv:2512.24271`  
  _Zhe Huang, Hao Wen, Aiming Hao, Bingze Song, Meiqi Wu, Jiahong Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made remarkable progress in video understanding. However, they suffer from a critical vulnerability: an over-reliance on language priors, which can lead to visual ungrounded hallucinations, especially when processing counterfactual videos that defy common sense. This limitation, stemming from the intrinsic data imbalance between text and video, is challenging to address due to the substantial cost of collecting and annotating counterfactual data. To address this, we introduce DualityForge, a novel counterfactual data synthesis framework that employs controllable, diffusion-based video editing to transform real-world videos into counterfactual scenarios. By embedding structured contextual information into the video editing and QA generation processes, the framework automatically produces high-quality QA pairs together with original-edited video pairs for contrastive training. Based on this, we build DualityVidQA, a large-scale video dataset designed to reduce MLLM hallucinations. In addition, to fully exploit the contrastive nature of our paired data, we propose Duality-Normalized Advantage Training (DNA-Train), a two-stage SFT-RL training regime where the RL phase applies pair-wise $\ell_1$ advantage normalization, thereby enabling a more stable and efficient policy optimization. Experiments on DualityVidQA-Test demonstrate that our method substantially reduces model hallucinations on counterfactual videos, yielding a relative improvement of 24.0% over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline. Moreover, our approach achieves significant gains across both hallucination and general-purpose benchmarks, indicating strong generalization capability. We will open-source our dataset and code.
  </details>

- **[Modular Neural Image Signal Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08564)**  `arXiv:2512.08564`  
  _Mahmoud Afifi, Zhongling Wang, Ran Zhang, Michael S. Brown_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural image signal processing (ISP) pipelines have largely abandoned the modular design of classical ISPs in favor of black-box networks, gaining expressiveness but losing interpretability, controllability, and the ability to swap or extend stages. Reintroducing modularity exposes a tradeoff: pipelines built from fixed operators or fixed neural proxies preserve interpretability but limit expressiveness, while jointly optimizing the proxies recovers expressiveness but often entangles functional roles across stages. We present a practical role-preserving and yet expressive neural ISP built on a two-level training strategy. At the module level, components with available ground truth are optimized separately to preserve functional decomposition. At the operator level, where intermediate ground truth is impractical to obtain, operators are trained jointly under final-image supervision but kept aligned with their roles via architectural design and role specific losses. The resulting framework is simultaneously interpretable, controllable, and expressive, enabling operator-level adjustment, targeted debugging, multi-style extension without full-pipeline retraining, and rendering of raw images from unseen cameras by swapping the camera specific modules. Lightweight at 0.5-3.9M parameters, our ISP achieves state-of-the-art results on most S24 picture styles and competitive performance on MIT-Adobe FiveK at a fraction of the parameter count of the closest neural ISPs. Code and the photo-editing tool are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[EditThinker: Enhancing Image Editors via Iterative Reasoning with a Plug-and-Play VLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05965)**  `arXiv:2512.05965`  
  _Hongyu Li, Manyuan Zhang, Dian Zheng, Ziyu Guo, Yimeng Jia, Kaituo Feng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image editors can produce realistic images while still failing to satisfy the requested changes. Improving their instruction following requires identifying these failures and translating visual feedback into instructions that the editor can execute. We introduce EditThinker, an 8B vision-language model (VLM) that enhances existing image editors through iterative reasoning while keeping their weights fixed. EditThinker jointly critiques semantic consistency and visual quality, reasons about editing failures, and refines the instruction in a structured response. It interacts with the editor through a Critique-Refine-Repeat loop, providing a plug-and-play interface for feedback-driven editing. Learning effective refinements requires more than imitating plausible expert suggestions: the instructions must work with the capabilities of the underlying editor. We therefore combine supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning from executed editing outcomes, using format, critic, and edit rewards. To support this training, we construct ThinkEdit-167k, a dataset of 167k step-wise samples with unified supervision for critique, reasoning, and instruction refinement. Across four tested editors, EditThinker improves overall scores on GEdit-Bench-EN, ImgEdit-Bench, RISE-Bench, and KRIS-Bench. Ablations examine the joint model design, data allocation, and training across VLM backbones. In our GEdit round-budget study, refinement achieves higher scores with fewer editor calls than best-of-N selection. We will release our data construction framework, datasets, and models.
  </details>

- **[FlowLUT: Efficient Image Enhancement via Differentiable LUTs and Iterative Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23608)**  `arXiv:2509.23608`  
  _Liubing Hu, Chen Wu, Anrui Wang, Dianjie Lu, Guijuan Zhang, Zhuoran Zheng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep learning-based image enhancement methods face a fundamental trade-off between computational efficiency and representational capacity. For example, although a conventional three-dimensional Look-Up Table (3D LUT) can process a degraded image in real time, it lacks representational flexibility and depends solely on a fixed prior. To address this problem, we introduce FlowLUT, a novel end-to-end model that integrates the efficiency of LUTs, multiple priors, and the parameter-independent characteristic of flow-matched reconstructed images. Specifically, firstly, the input image is transformed in color space by a collection of differentiable 3D LUTs (containing a large number of 3D LUTs with different priors). Subsequently, a lightweight content-aware dynamically predicts fusion weights, enabling scene-adaptive color correction with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ complexity. Next, a lightweight fusion prediction network runs on multiple 3D LUTs, with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ complexity for scene-adaptive colorthis http URL, to address the inherent representation limitations of LUTs, we design an innovative iterative flow matching method to restore local structural details and eliminate artifacts. Finally, the entire model is jointly optimized under a composite loss function enforcing perceptual and structural fidelity. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[Rethinking Multiplication in Neural Networks with Hadamard Transform-Assisted Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23103)**  `arXiv:2509.23103`  
  _Emadeldeen Hamdan, Marouane Tliba, Ulas Bagci, Ahmet Enis Cetin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multiplication-avoiding neural operators are attractive for compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures, but directly replacing conventional convolutions often causes accuracy degradation. We investigate whether this limitation arises from multiplication avoidance itself or from the representation on which the operator acts. In this work, we introduce Hadamard Transform-assisted multiplication-avoiding (HMA) operators that combine Walsh--Hadamard transform features with multiplication-avoiding channel mixing. To identify where conventional multiplication remains necessary, we employ a gated formulation in which conventional and HMA operators compete through learned layer-wise coefficients. ResNet-18 experiments show that intermediate convolutional layers assign greater weight to HMA, whereas the earliest layers and final classifier retain greater contribution from conventional computation. Guided by this observation, we construct a compact hybrid HMA network and train it using knowledge distillation from a conventional teacher. On CIFAR-10, the resulting ResNet-18 student achieves 91.2\% accuracy compared with 90.4\% for the corresponding conventional baseline while reducing parameters by 68.25\%, conventional MACs by 85.71\%, and general multiplications by 85.54\%. Across ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, HMA with knowledge distillation matches or improves the conventional models. These results show that Hadamard-domain feature restructuring can improve the accuracy--complexity tradeoff of multiplication-avoiding networks and provide a practical path toward efficient CIM inference.
  </details>

- **[Concepts in Motion: Temporal Concept Bottleneck Model for Interpretable Video Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20899)**  `arXiv:2509.20899`  
  _Patrick Knab, Sascha Marton, Philipp J. Schubert, Drago Guggiana, Christian Bartelt_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enable interpretable image classification by structuring predictions around human-understandable concepts, but extending this paradigm to video remains challenging due to the difficulty of extracting concepts and modeling them over time. In this paper, we introduce MoTIF (Moving Temporal Interpretable Framework), a transformer-based concept architecture that operates on sequences of temporally grounded concept activations, by employing per-concept temporal self-attention to model when individual concepts recur and how their temporal patterns contribute to predictions. Central to the framework is a class-conditioned VLM-based concept discovery module that extracts object- and action-centric textual concepts from training videos, yielding temporally expressive concept sets without manual concept annotation. Across multiple video benchmarks, this combination improves over global concept bottlenecks and remains competitive within the interpretable concept-bottleneck setting, while narrowing the gap to strong black-box video baselines that we report as contextual references. Code available atthis http URL.
  </details>

- **[SEER-VAR: Semantic Egocentric Environment Reasoner for Vehicle Augmented Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17255)**  `arXiv:2508.17255`  
  _Yuzhi Lai, Shenghai Yuan, Peizheng Li, Jun Lou, Zhouyu Ran, Andreas Zell_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present SEER-VAR, a novel framework for egocentric vehicle-based augmented reality (AR) that unifies semantic decomposition, Context-Aware SLAM Branches (CASB), and LLM-driven recommendation. Unlike existing systems that assume static or single-view settings, SEER-VAR dynamically separates cabin and road scenes via depth-guided vision-language grounding. Two SLAM branches track egocentric motion in each context, while a GPT-based module generates context-aware overlays such as dashboard cues and hazard alerts. To support evaluation, we introduce EgoSLAM-Drive, a real-world dataset featuring synchronized egocentric views, 6DoF ground-truth poses, and AR annotations across diverse driving scenarios. Experiments demonstrate that SEER-VAR achieves robust spatial alignment and perceptually coherent AR rendering across varied environments. As one of the first to explore LLM-based AR recommendation in egocentric driving, we address the lack of comparable systems through structured prompting and detailed user studies. Results show that SEER-VAR enhances perceived scene understanding, overlay relevance, and driver ease, providing an effective foundation for future research in this direction. Code and dataset will be made open source.
  </details>

- **[TimeMachine: Fine-Grained Facial Age Editing with Identity Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11284)**  `arXiv:2508.11284`  
  _Yilin Mi, Qixin Yan, Zheng-Peng Duan, Chunle Guo, Hubery Yin, Hao Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  With the advancement of generative models, facial image editing has made significant progress. However, achieving fine-grained age editing while preserving personal identity remains a challenging task. In this paper, we propose TimeMachine, a unified diffusion-based framework for accurate facial age editing with identity preservation. TimeMachine employs fine-grained age conditions and a Multi-Cross-Attention module to decouple the dedicated age and identity conditions. This branch-wise design enables controllable age transformation while maintaining identity consistency. Furthermore, we introduce an Age Classifier Guidance (ACG) module that predicts age embeddings from latent denoising features without reconstructing images during training. This lightweight training-only predictor provides additional age-related supervision and is removed during inference. To support large-scale training, we construct HFFA (High-quality Fine-grained Facial-Age), a million-scale collection of high-resolution face images annotated with captions, identity embeddings, MiVOLO-estimated numerical ages, and age embeddings. Extensive experiments across five public face datasets demonstrate that TimeMachine achieves superior age accuracy and identity preservation relative to the evaluated baselines, with consistent conclusions across five age estimators.
  </details>

- **[Sample-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Medical Image-to-Image Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00766)**  `arXiv:2508.00766`  
  _Irene Iele, Francesco Di Feola, Matteo Tortora, Rosa Sicilia, Valerio Guarrasi, Paolo Soda_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image-to-image translation has emerged as a powerful technique in medical imaging, enabling tasks such as image denoising and cross-modality conversion. However, it suffers from limitations in handling out-of-distribution samples without causing performance degradation. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) framework that dynamically adjusts the translation process based on the characteristics of each test sample. Our method introduces a Reconstruction Module to quantify the domain shift and a Dynamic Adaptation Block that selectively modifies the internal features of a pretrained translation model to mitigate the shift without compromising the performance on in-distribution samples that do not require adaptation. We evaluate our approach on two medical image-to-image translation tasks: low-dose CT denoising and T1 to T2 MRI translation, showing consistent improvements over both the baseline translation model without TTA and prior TTA methods. Our analysis highlights the limitations of the state-of-the-art that uniformly apply the adaptation to both out-of-distribution and in-distribution samples, demonstrating that dynamic, sample-specific adjustment offers a promising path to improve model resilience in real-world scenarios. The code is available at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[A2Mamba: Attention-augmented State Space Models for Visual Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16624)**  `arXiv:2507.16624`  
  _Meng Lou, Yunxiang Fu, Yizhou Yu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Transformers and Mamba, initially invented for natural language processing, have inspired backbone architectures for visual recognition. Recent studies integrated Local Attention Transformers with Mamba to capture both local details and global contexts. Despite competitive performance, these methods are limited to simple stacking of Transformer and Mamba layers without any interaction mechanism between them. Thus, deep integration between Transformer and Mamba layers remains an open problem. We address this problem by proposing A2Mamba, a powerful Transformer-Mamba hybrid network architecture, featuring a new token mixer termed Multi-scale Attention-augmented State Space Model (MASS), where multi-scale attention maps are integrated into an attention-augmented SSM (A2SSM). A key step of A2SSM performs a variant of cross-attention by spatially aggregating the SSM's hidden states using the multi-scale attention maps, which enhances spatial dependencies pertaining to a two-dimensional space while improving the dynamic modeling capabilities of SSMs. Our A2Mamba outperforms all previous ConvNet-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based architectures in visual recognition tasks. For instance, A2Mamba-L achieves an impressive 86.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. In semantic segmentation, A2Mamba-B exceeds CAFormer-S36 by 2.5% in mIoU, while exhibiting higher efficiency. In object detection and instance segmentation with Cascade Mask R-CNN, A2Mamba-S surpasses MambaVision-B by 1.2%/0.9% in AP^b/AP^m, while having 40% fewer parameters. Code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[ZIP: Scalable Crowd Counting via Zero-Inflated Poisson Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19955)**  `arXiv:2506.19955`  
  _Yiming Ma, Victor Sanchez, Tanaya Guha_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The majority of crowd counting methods directly regress blockwise density maps using losses based on Mean Squared Error (MSE). This practice has two critical limitations: 1) it fails to account for the extreme spatial sparsity of annotations (i.e., over 95% of standard $8\times8$ blocks are empty across most benchmarks), which makes supervision signals in informative regions diluted by the predominant zeros. 2) MSE corresponds to a Gaussian error model that poorly matches discrete, non-negative count data. We introduce a novel crowd counting framework that is scalable and directly addresses the above limitations. This framework, named ZIP, models blockwise counts with a Zero-Inflated Poisson likelihood: A zero-inflation term models excess zeros in sparse annotations, while the Poisson component captures expected counts while respecting their discrete, non-negative nature. We provide a generalization analysis showing that the ZIP negative log-likelihood (NLL) has the same order of uniform generalization gap as Poisson NLL while offering a richer zero-inflated likelihood family, and that its bound scales more favorably with the number of spatial blocks than optimal-transport-based supervision. To assess the scalability and broad applicability of ZIP, we apply the same formulation across diverse backbones, from lightweight models to high-capacity architectures, spanning more than $100\times$ in both parameter count and inference FLOPs. Experiments on four standard crowd-counting benchmarks show that ZIP achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across a wide range of backbone capacities. Although ZIP is designed for sparse blockwise count maps, it also remains effective in dense crowd scenes, reducing MAE and RMSE by 3.9% and 8.5%, respectively, over mPrompt on UCF-QNRF. Code and trained weights are available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[AIR: Rethinking Image-Text Offset Alignment in Multimodal Contrastive Representation Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10895)**  `arXiv:2506.10895`  
  _Guimeng Liu, Milad Abdollahzadeh, Ngai-Man Cheung_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Image-text offset alignment, which refers to the consistency between visual transformation directions and their corresponding textual transformation directions, has become an important relational property in multimodal contrastive representation spaces such as CLIP and SigLIP. This property plays a central role in text-driven visual transformation tasks, including generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing, where textual offsets are used to guide visual transformations. These methods fundamentally rely on the assumption that image and text offsets are well aligned, such that textual transformation directions can provide reliable guidance for corresponding visual transformations. However, the validity of this alignment assumption has not been systematically examined. In this work, we question this foundational assumption by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of image-text offset alignment in multimodal contrastive representation space. Our findings reveal not only noticeable offset misalignment but also a meaningful positive correlation between image-text offset misalignment and semantic concept distance across six large datasets and eight contrastive vision-language models. Based on this discovery, we propose Adaptation with Iterative Refinement (AIR), a method that iteratively refines text offsets through anchor sampling and our proposed concept description learning to mitigate the downstream effect of image-text offset misalignment and improve guidance accuracy. Comprehensive experiments on zero-shot generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing across 40 setups, including qualitative, quantitative, and user studies, consistently show that AIR enables state-of-the-art performance in these tasks.
  </details>

- **[VFRTok: Variable Frame Rates Video Tokenizer with Duration-Proportional Information Assumption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12053)**  `arXiv:2505.12053`  
  _Tianxiong Zhong, Xingye Tian, Boyuan Jiang, Xuebo Wang, Xin Tao, Pengfei Wan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern video generation frameworks based on Latent Diffusion Models suffer from inefficiencies in tokenization due to the Frame-Proportional Information Assumption. Existing tokenizers provide fixed temporal compression rates, causing the computational cost of the diffusion model to scale linearly with the frame rate. The paper proposes the Duration-Proportional Information Assumption: the upper bound on the information capacity of a video is proportional to the duration rather than the number of frames. Based on this insight, the paper introduces VFRTok, a Transformer-based video tokenizer, that enables variable frame rate encoding and decoding through asymmetric frame rate training between the encoder and decoder. Furthermore, the paper proposes Partial Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to decouple position and content modeling, which groups correlated patches into unified tokens. The Partial RoPE effectively improves content-awareness, enhancing the video generation capability. Benefiting from the compact and continuous spatio-temporal representation, VFRTok achieves competitive reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art generation fidelity while using only 1/8 tokens compared to existing tokenizers. The code and weights are released at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Persistence-based Line Detection in Hough Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16114)**  `arXiv:2504.16114`  
  _Johannes Ferner, Stefan Huber, Saverio Messineo, Angel Pop, Martin Uray_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Hough transform is a popular and classical technique in computer vision for the detection of lines (or more general objects). It maps a pixel into a dual space -- the Hough space: each pixel is mapped to the set of lines through this pixel, which forms a curve in Hough space. The detection of lines then becomes a voting process to find those lines that received many votes by pixels. However, this voting is done by thresholding, which is susceptible to noise and other artifacts. In this work, we present an alternative voting technique to detect peaks in the Hough space based on persistent homology, which very naturally addresses limitations of simple thresholding. Experiments on synthetic data show that our method significantly outperforms the original method, while also demonstrating enhanced robustness. This work seeks to inspire future research in two key directions. First, we highlight the untapped potential of Topological Data Analysis techniques and advocate for their broader integration into existing methods, including well-established ones. Secondly, we initiate a discussion on the mathematical stability of the Hough transform, encouraging exploration of mathematically grounded improvements to enhance its robustness.
  </details>

- **[Mamba-3D as Masked Autoencoders for Accurate and Data-Efficient Analysis of Medical Ultrasound Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20258)**  `arXiv:2503.20258`  
  _Jiaheng Zhou, Yanfeng Zhou, Wei Fang, Yuxing Tang, Le Lu, Ge Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Ultrasound videos are an important form of clinical imaging data, and deep learning-based automated analysis can improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical efficiency. However, the scarcity of labeled data and the inherent challenges of video analysis have impeded the advancement of related methods. In this work, we introduce E-ViM$^3$, a data-efficient Vision Mamba network that preserves the 3D structure of video data, enhancing long-range dependencies and inductive biases to better model space-time correlations. With our design of Enclosure Global Tokens (EGT), the model captures and aggregates global features more effectively than competing methods. To further improve data efficiency, we employ masked video modeling for self-supervised pre-training, with the proposed Spatial-Temporal Chained (STC) masking strategy designed to adapt to various video scenarios. Experiments demonstrate that E-ViM$^3$ performs as the state-of-the-art in two high-level semantic analysis tasks across four datasets of varying sizes: EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS, MICCAI-BUV, and WHBUS. Furthermore, our model achieves competitive performance with limited labels, highlighting its potential impact on real-world clinical applications.
  </details>

- **[MMGenBench: An Automated Pipeline for Evaluating LMMs from a Text-to-Image Generation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14062)**  `arXiv:2411.14062`  
  _Hailang Huang, Yong Wang, Zixuan Huang, Huaqiu Li, Tongwen Huang, Xiangxiang Chu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing benchmarks often rely on predefined questions or reference captions, limiting their flexibility for evaluating detailed descriptions on new image collections. We present MMGenBench, an automated benchmark framework for evaluating Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) from raw images without per-image questions or reference captions. The pipeline generates descriptions, reconstructs images with a frozen text-to-image model, and compares the original and reconstructed images using a frozen image encoder. It produces reusable per-image scores and inspectable reconstructions, supporting both model comparison and diagnosis of reconstructible visual information. We construct MMGenBench-Domain with 10,000 generated images and MMGenBench-Test with 1,284 images spanning 13 overlapping visual patterns. Evaluation of 68 LMMs reveals pattern-specific differences in reconstruction quality that overall scores can obscure. On 1,000 human-labeled caption pairs from six models, the default score achieves 90.00\% sample-level agreement. Factual perturbations and component analyses characterize the score's sensitivity under the evaluated pipeline, while a COCO study provides initial validation on natural photographs. MMGenBench complements existing benchmarks by linking automated comparisons to visual evidence of the information preserved in LMM descriptions. Project page:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Revisiting Out-of-Distribution Detection in Semantic Difference Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11254)**  `arXiv:2411.11254`  
  _Xingming Long, Jie Zhang, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The primary goal of most existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection works is to identify inputs with "Semantic Shifts". However, the existing definition of "Semantic Shift" in previous studies remains vague, resulting in controversial choices of OOD samples in many benchmarks. Consequently, some benchmarks are too trivial for evaluating OOD detection, whereas others include OOD instances that are practically undetectable. In this paper, we propose a formal definition of "Semantic Difference Space", which reflects the scope of a model's OOD detection capability after training convergence. The definition is grounded in an analysis of how the loss-based optimization shapes the model's perceptual toward OOD inputs, offering theoretical explanations for the controversies regarding the selection of OOD samples across existing benchmarks. To validate the correctness of our analysis, we construct multiple datasets, primarily in the context of image classification, and we find that compared to different OOD detection methods, different OOD settings play a more decisive role in the detection results. Finally, we propose a simple yet effective OOD Separability Probe (OSP) method to evaluate whether the existing OOD detection benchmarks are reasonable, identifying issues in some benchmarks and highlighting a few that are worth further exploration.
  </details>

- **[Retinexformer: One-stage Retinex-based Transformer for Low-light Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.06705)**  `arXiv:2303.06705`  
  _Yuanhao Cai, Hao Bian, Jing Lin, Haoqian Wang, Radu Timofte, Yulun Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When enhancing low-light images, many deep learning algorithms are based on the Retinex theory. However, the Retinex model does not consider the corruptions hidden in the dark or introduced by the light-up process. Besides, these methods usually require a tedious multi-stage training pipeline and rely on convolutional neural networks, showing limitations in capturing long-range dependencies. In this paper, we formulate a simple yet principled One-stage Retinex-based Framework (ORF). ORF first estimates the illumination information to light up the low-light image and then restores the corruption to produce the enhanced image. We design an Illumination-Guided Transformer (IGT) that utilizes illumination representations to direct the modeling of non-local interactions of regions with different lighting conditions. By plugging IGT into ORF, we obtain our algorithm, Retinexformer. Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our Retinexformer significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on thirteen benchmarks. The user study and application on low-light object detection also reveal the latent practical values of our method. Code, models, and results are available atthis https URL. Our project page atthis https URLshows more visual results. An online Gradio demo is available on Hugging Face atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[HindSight: A Graph-Based Vision Model Architecture For Representing Part-Whole Hierarchies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03722)**  `arXiv:2104.03722`  
  _Muhammad AbdurRafae_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper presents a model architecture for encoding the representations of part-whole hierarchies in images in form of a graph. The idea is to divide the image into patches of different levels and then treat all of these patches as nodes for a fully connected graph. A dynamic feature extraction module is used to extract feature representations from these patches in each graph iteration. This enables us to learn a rich graph representation of the image that encompasses the inherent part-whole hierarchical information. Utilizing proper self-supervised training techniques, such a model can be trained as a general purpose vision encoder model which can then be used for various vision related downstream tasks (e.g., Image Classification, Object Detection, Image Captioning, etc.).
  </details>

- **[A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33133)**  `arXiv:2611.33133`  
  _Hussamuddin Syed_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
  </details>

- **[Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33111)**  `arXiv:2611.33111`  
  _Yuxing Liu, Wei Zuo, Walid Krichene, Tong Zhang, Li Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.
  </details>

- **[Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33102)**  `arXiv:2611.33102`  
  _Jiayi Sheng, Jingwen Gu, Guanning Zeng, Zhaoyi Zhou, Stefano Viel, Qianqian Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.
  </details>

- **[GREMLIN: Generating Random Environments for Meta-Learning with Interacting Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33101)**  `arXiv:2611.33101`  
  _Octave Gaspard_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Can randomly parameterized neural environments supply useful experience for learning a reinforcement learning algorithm? We investigate this question using DiscoRL's rule-discovery framework, replacing human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments. Each game combines bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward. After 224.8 million agent-environment steps, we froze the teacher and trained fresh agents. DQN outscored GREMLIN on most games, both generated and human-designed. GREMLIN nevertheless outperformed the untrained teacher on all 26 games, showing that generated experience can improve a learning rule. It remains unclear whether this approach can yield a competitive rule with longer meta-training.
  </details>

- **[Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33080)**  `arXiv:2611.33080`  
  _Yufeng Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput ofthis http URLon a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
  </details>

- **[Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33062)**  `arXiv:2611.33062`  
  _Saket Gollapudi, Elisa Bertino, Sewoong Oh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $\epsilon$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $\eta$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $\eta c =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Local Indices Are Not Enough: Synchrony and Global Information in Bandit Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33056)**  `arXiv:2611.33056`  
  _Aakash Gore, Shivaram Kalyanakrishnan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Standard index-based stochastic bandit algorithms such as KL-UCB and Thompson Sampling achieve optimal $O(\log T)$ regret over a horizon $T$. The former uses the global timestep to construct each arm's index, while the latter samples each arm's belief distribution at every timestep. The necessity of global information and synchronous index updates for achieving optimal regret has not been examined yet. In this paper, we investigate the fundamental limits of asynchronous local index algorithms---those that recalculate an arm's index only upon pulling it, using solely that arm's own reward history and a local randomness budget. We prove that no such algorithm can achieve $O(\log T)$ regret across all bandit instances. We then analyse the functional equations arising from asynchronous updates, and show that the achievable regret lies in a sub-polynomial, super-polylogarithmic regime. We propose an asynchronous local index policy whose regret upper bound also lies in this regime. Turning to synchronous local algorithms, which sample every arm's index at all timesteps as in Thompson Sampling, we show that a locally determined randomness budget per arm suffices to retain $O(\log T)$ regret, demonstrating that synchrony, albeit with some randomness, is essential to the optimality of Thompson Sampling.
  </details>

- **[Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33048)**  `arXiv:2611.33048`  
  _Yanlai Yang, Minki Kang, Divyam Madaan, Sung Ju Hwang, Mengye Ren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.
  </details>

- **[Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33031)**  `arXiv:2611.33031`  
  _Steffen Urban_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Best Arm Identification with Unknown Post-Action Context Distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33024)**  `arXiv:2611.33024`  
  _Amir Mohammad Abouei, Mohammad Shahverdikondori, Emad Emamjomeh, Negar Kiyavash_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study best arm identification (BAI) with post-action context in the fixed-confidence setting. After choosing an action, the learner observes a post-action context together with a reward whose distribution depends only on this context. Incorporating such intermediate information can substantially reduce the sample complexity of identifying the best arm. While Shahverdikondori et al. (2026a) analyzed the case where the distribution of contexts given actions is known, we address the more challenging and practically relevant case where this distribution is unknown. We derive an instance-dependent sample complexity lower bound and propose a Track-and-Stop algorithm that matches it asymptotically with access to an optimization oracle. Our stopping rule uses a new concentration inequality that jointly controls uncertainty in the context distributions and reward means, removing the factor of two incurred by separate concentration bounds. Implementing the algorithm generally requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. We propose a convex relaxation with instance-dependent approximation guarantees, including asymptotic tightness on hard Gaussian instances. Experiments demonstrate that exploiting post-action context reduces the sample complexity relative to baselines that ignore it, even when the context distributions are unknown.
  </details>

- **[PAC-style Bounds on the Conditional Validity of Conformal Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33023)**  `arXiv:2611.33023`  
  _Nicolo Colombo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conformal prediction sets are guaranteed to be marginally valid over the attribute space, but local coverage can diverge from the user-defined target $1-\alpha$. Constructing conditionally valid prediction sets with finite calibration data is impossible for a general data-generating distribution. We derive PAC-type probabilistic lower bounds on the input-conditional coverage of any conformal predictor, without assumptions on the data distribution.
