After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. Therefore, high classification performance on this benchmark does not come only from learning the exact defect configuration.
  </details>

- **[Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31271)**  `arXiv:2611.31271`  
  _Fazl Barez, Tung-Yu Wu, Iván Arcuschin, Michael Lan, Vincent Wang, Noah Siegel, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Chain-of-thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi-step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading and are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model's underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.
  </details>

- **[Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31249)**  `arXiv:2611.31249`  
  _Jie Peng, Davis Hobley, Song Wang, Zachary PlotkinB, Tianlong Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.
  </details>

- **[Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30986)**  `arXiv:2611.30986`  
  _Yihong Luo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30634)**  `arXiv:2611.30634`  
  _Da Xiao, Qingye Meng, Shengping Li, Xingyuan Yuan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Vasicek Graph Diffusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30605)**  `arXiv:2611.30605`  
  _Junyi Tang, Chang Liu, Kun Zhan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion-based graph generation models progressively transform Gaussian noise into structured graphs through stochastic dynamics. We observe that the effectiveness of this transformation is fundamentally determined by the evolution of the diffusion trajectory. Existing graph diffusion models often suffer from excessive uncertainty during diffusion and delayed growth of the signal-to-noise ratio, causing useful structural information to emerge only in the later stages of generation. To address this issue, we propose the Vasicek Graph Diffusion (VGD), a graph diffusion process derived from the Vasicek dynamics. The key insight of VGD is data-anchored mean dynamics with a closed-form solution, which analytically establishes a continuous transition from Gaussian noise to the target graph distribution. Unlike conventional graph diffusion processes that rely predominantly on stochastic evolution, VGD introduces a data-anchored drift that continuously steers the latent state toward the target distribution throughout diffusion. As a consequence, VGD maintains a smoothly evolving uncertainty while rapidly increasing the signal-to-noise ratio throughout diffusion, allowing informative graph structures to emerge much earlier during generation. Extensive experiments on multiple graph generation benchmarks demonstrate that VGD outperforms existing diffusion-based graph generative models in terms of generation quality and structural fidelity.
  </details>

- **[De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30509)**  `arXiv:2611.30509`  
  _Kexin Zhang, Manhao Guan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.
  </details>

- **[Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28621)**  `arXiv:2611.28621`  
  _Yukinori Yamamoto, Kotaro Yoshida, Ryotaro Shimizu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27376)**  `arXiv:2611.27376`  
  _Zhen Zhang, Changyi Yang, Xuehai He, Chengzhi Liu, Yutong Yin, Ziyue Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.
  </details>

- **[Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25594)**  `arXiv:2611.25594`  
  _Xinze Shi, Litian Zhang, Zhenjie Su, Zelong Yu, Yuting Zhang, Chaozhuo Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.
  </details>

- **[Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23570)**  `arXiv:2611.23570`  
  _Xinyang Li, Chih-Hsuan Yang, Xiaolong Ma, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Vikram Vasudevan, Rajeev Thakur, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.
  </details>

- **[LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22757)**  `arXiv:2611.22757`  
  _Weizhong Huang, Huaijia Kou, Yan Zhang, Fei Chao, Xiawu Zheng, Liujuan Cao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.
  </details>

- **[On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19207)**  `arXiv:2611.19207`  
  _Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Yi Yu, Gongli Xi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.
  </details>

- **[Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17772)**  `arXiv:2611.17772`  
  _Anh Tu Ngo, Anupam Chattopadhyay_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployments where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. The framework allows hosts to customize the target defensive styles and switch among them per request, thereby making it harder for adversaries to identify a stable, learnable signature. Because this inference-time intervention largely preserves answer correctness and avoids the degenerate artifacts of prior defenses, adversaries are misled into believing they are extracting valid teacher outputs. Meanwhile, standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that the framework consistently degrades student learning across model families, with minimal inference overhead. Our approach serves as a low-cost deterrent that raises the attacker's extraction and post-hoc sanitization costs. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12016)**  `arXiv:2611.12016`  
  _Shayan Talaei, Agam Bhatia, Arshia Soltani Moakhar, Jonas Hübotter, Amin Saberi, Azalia Mirhoseini_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.
  </details>

- **[Alleviating Limited Effectiveness and Multi-Class Collapse in Deep Graph-level Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06052)**  `arXiv:2611.06052`  
  _Xiaoyang Lin, Renchi Yang, Yuqi Chen, Xin Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Given a collection of $N$ graphs, graph-level clustering (GLC) seeks to partition the $N$ graphs into semantically meaningful groups, which serves as a fundamental task in analyzing graph-structured data. While Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) have become the de facto encoders for GLC, they still fail to distinguish graphs due to their neglect of global topology. On top of that, existing deep clustering frameworks suffer from severe "clustering collapse" issues, particularly in imbalanced multi-class scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose S$^3$GLC, a novel framework that integrates global topological characteristics with local neighborhood features for balanced GLC. Theoretically, we leverage the Hoffman-Wielandt inequality to construct Spectral Signature as a rigorous lower bound for graph edit distance (GED), providing a computationally efficient proxy for global topological features. We additionally propose a joint manifold-preserving sparse regression module to fuse Spectral Signature with Spatial Representation, eliminating noise while preserving the complementary information. Furthermore, to mitigate clustering collapse, we introduce a balanced clustering objective based on optimal transport, harnessing the Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization to enforce equipartition constraints on cluster assignments. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that S$^3$GLC significantly outperforms 15 state-of-the-art baselines, achieving remarkable improvements on benchmark datasets such as REDDIT-12K and OGBG-PPA.
  </details>

- **[Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01168)**  `arXiv:2611.01168`  
  _Hiroki Hasegawa, Yukihiko Okada_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Iterative estimators for low Tucker rank tensors, such as HOOI, nuclear-norm proximal and ADMM methods, Frank-Wolfe and scaled gradient descent, form large objects in every iteration: unfoldings, Kronecker operators, full SVDs and ambient iterates. The update uses little of these objects, yet they make memory the limiting resource on large tensors and on edge-sized devices. Remedies for each of these costs are known. However, it is unclear when a rewriting keeps the iterates unchanged, and where it pays off against efficient implementations. We therefore present a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation. First, we state exactness as an intertwining relation between the stored state and the reference iteration. Second, we show that three known components satisfy this relation for five estimators: computing only the singular triplets that an update needs, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states. As a result, the iterates and all guarantees of the reference estimator stay the same. On an A100 GPU, with the input data counted in the memory, lightweight HOOI needs the least memory of 15 HOOI-type methods at every size ($95\times$ less beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on $800^3$ tensors), and it is the fastest method that reaches the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, ours is faster and lighter for three of five estimators. On a surveillance video and a satellite hyperspectral cube, ours is the only implementation that fits a 1 GiB and a 4 GiB device. Finally, we show that the memory and time gains need separate conditions, and we identify where these conditions fail.
  </details>

- **[Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00606)**  `arXiv:2611.00606`  
  _Karl Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.
  </details>

- **[Tiered Cache Blocking and In-Kernel Task Dispatch for Long-Context Prefill Attention on CPU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38809)**  `arXiv:2610.38809`  
  _Kwun Fung Lau, Frost Mitchell, Kanya Mo, Emani Ashok_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce TACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. TACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
  </details>

- **[ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35955)**  `arXiv:2610.35955`  
  _Ning Yang, Bohan Cui, Zhuowen Liu, Yuting Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
  </details>

- **[HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24501)**  `arXiv:2610.24501`  
  _Zhaodong Guo, Haoyun Feng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.
  </details>

- **[The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22650)**  `arXiv:2610.22650`  
  _Xinyu Zhao, Davis Wertheimer, Ashutosh Sharma, Rameswar Panda, Paul Pu Liang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Finally, we investigate whether our findings extend to RL via experiments on our 1.2B models as well as Qwen3-1.7B and 4B, and find that AdamW and Muon achieve comparable final performance in math RLVR. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.
  </details>

- **[SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17029)**  `arXiv:2610.17029`  
  _Lucas Thil, Jesse Read, Guillaume Doquet, Rim Kaddah_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable, and growth recovers only mechanisms the pretrained network represents. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; on Navier-Stokes they compose close to their supervised counterparts.
  </details>

- **[Noise Your Prompt: Noising Conditioning Tokens in Continuous Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09145)**  `arXiv:2610.09145`  
  _Justin Jung_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We revisit a standard accepted practice in the continuous diffusion language model literature of fixing conditioning prompt tokens clean during training. We make a very simple modification: also noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training. We demonstrate that under this modified training objective, we achieve better generalization in combinatorial reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and N-Queens, with the largest gains on harder variants ($3.73\% \to 24.65\%$ solve rate on Sudoku Hard), and increased diversity of generated solutions ($50.60\% \to 73.79\%$ coverage on 10x10 N-Queens). We also show measurable improvements to natural language generation quality in modest dataset regimes with Gigaword summarization, but notably demonstrate that gains do not transfer to all natural language tasks (e.g open ended dialogue generation). Our method is a single line change to the training objective, requires no additional inference costs by default, and provides the flexibility of classifier-free guidance inspired guided sampling. Our \href{this https URL}{code} is publicly available.
  </details>

- **[Convex-Concave Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09108)**  `arXiv:2610.09108`  
  _Shripad V. Deshmukh, Yaswanth Chittepu, Dhawal Gupta, Philip Thomas, Scott Niekum_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[\pi/\pi_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and establish inner-loop descent and limit-point stationarity for the theoretical algorithm, together with a conditional outer-loop performance bound. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO on classic control, and on a clinically motivated, stochastic, mid-horizon sepsis simulator converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve. The code is publicly available at:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Beyond Accuracy: Prefix-Invariant Realizations of Low-Precision Fast Matrix Multiplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39816)**  `arXiv:2609.39816`  
  _Shuxiao Xie, Shuyang Xie, Yuan Cao, Dezhi Ran, Wei Yang, Tao Xie_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fast matrix multiplication saves multiplications through exact cancellation, but rounding sums that mix token rows can leave contributions from later tokens in earlier language model outputs. This threatens prefix invariance, which likelihood scoring and batched inference rely on: an output must depend only on its allowed prefix. On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, two fast FP8 realizations repaired to near-bf16 accuracy, and the existing fast kernel FalconGEMM, change answers when only text outside the allowed prefix is replaced: on 4.17--10.00% of OpenBookQA items scored by likelihood and 39.6--51.8% of NQ-open questions answered in a batch. Accuracy thus does not certify prefix invariance, and the stability criteria we analyze cannot tell realizations apart: across all 512 sign variants of two-level Strassen the criteria stay constant while teacher-forced perplexities span a 772.4$\times$ range on the same model. We therefore construct certified realizations of two-level Strassen on bounded integer codes that quantize token rows independently, then mix and cancel exactly before rescaling, using 49 block multiplications instead of 64. Our certificate guarantees bitwise equality to a prescribed row-local classical int8 operator at the same quantization specification, so every certified realization inherits its prefix invariance. Certification thus turns realization choice into a pure cost decision: which certified realization runs can no longer change any output. With optimized kernels, certified realizations run faster than classical int8 on an NVIDIA H20, and in the SGLang serving engine they raise throughput over its FP8 path by 1.2--5.6% on four models.
  </details>

- **[Server-Side Surrogate Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38833)**  `arXiv:2609.38833`  
  _Sungmin Kang, Zhengzhong Tu, Sunwoo Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) must learn new classes over time without forgetting the earlier ones. Existing replay methods counter forgetting on the clients, which store exemplars or train on synthetic samples. This burdens resource-constrained clients with extra memory and computation, and since each client stores exemplars only of the classes it has seen, the replay of earlier tasks stays as skewed as its local data. We propose ReSCENE, which moves replay entirely to the server. Each client uploads a few condensed surrogates per class, and the server keeps those of earlier tasks from all clients and trains the global model on them together with the current task, so the replay is balanced across all earlier classes. Since the global model and the surrogates co-evolve within a task, the surrogates of later rounds lie closer to the real data, so we introduce temporal herding, which compresses the pool of each task into a bounded buffer centered on the recent rounds, and establish a condition under which this buffer represents the task data more closely than keeping all surrogates. Across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, ReSCENE attains the highest average accuracy against eight baselines in all nine settings, by up to $31.1$ points, while requiring as little as $0.11\times$ of the client computation and up to $179\times$ less upload than the model-update baselines. ReSCENE stays ahead with more clients and larger models while keeping client cost low.
  </details>

- **[Can We Predict kNN-Based Anomalous Sound Detection Performance from Embedding-Space Geometry?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26460)**  `arXiv:2609.26460`  
  _Kevin Wilkinghoff, Zheng-Hua Tan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Anomaly detection systems are often trained using normal data alone, while model selection and evaluation typically require labeled anomalies. We study anomaly-free selection for k-nearest neighbor (kNN)-based anomaly detectors operating on embedding spaces, using pretrained audio representations and temporal pooling for first-shot industrial anomalous sound detection as a practically relevant application. We derive a lower bound on the area under the ROC curve (AUC) at the score level and use it to analyze kNN-based detection, relating score variability to the geometry of the embedding space. Under a local scaling model, we characterize how density variation, intrinsic-dimensional heterogeneity, and cross-domain mismatch contribute to inlier-score variability, and show how local density-based score normalization (LDN) affects these contributions. We then investigate anomaly-free model selection and show that inlier score variance alone does not reliably predict performance across different representations. To address this limitation, we introduce simple pseudo-anomaly probes that provide a reference for estimating relative score separation. Experiments on the DCASE 2022-2025 benchmarks, spanning four pretrained audio encoders and 208 candidate systems evaluate both kNN and LDN. The results show that LDN improves detection performance, while pseudo-anomaly-based estimators substantially improve anomaly-free model selection. The AUC Bound provides robust selection across pseudo-anomaly constructions, and a simple metadata-free construction offers a competitive alternative to existing approaches, even outperforming conventional development-set selection when combined with LDN.
  </details>

- **[SAVOR: Score Once, Learn Deeper in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24141)**  `arXiv:2609.24141`  
  _Keye Zheng, Hanyu Li, Yuan Gao, Zhan Cheng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own samples with token-level scores from a stronger teacher, and it effectively transfers reasoning ability to small language models. Each training step pays for student rollouts and teacher scoring, yet common OPD configurations make a single pass over the scored batch and then discard it. We observe that reusing the batch alone is not enough, because no single fixed teacher target suits every batch. In our runs, a fixed $\alpha$ of 0.3 exceeds a KL envelope at every training step, while 0.2 leaves over a quarter of it unused. We propose SAVOR, which selects for each batch the strongest teacher target inside the KL envelope, freezes the scored batch, and reuses it for a fixed number of student updates without further teacher calls. On five math reasoning benchmarks with a 1.7B student and a 30B-A3B teacher, SAVOR raises macro accuracy over TOP-D from 15.41 to 17.78 with two passes and to 19.36 with three passes at about the same teacher budget. With three passes, SAVOR nearly matches the final accuracy of TOP-D after one third of training while using 67.2% fewer teacher-scored tokens. These results suggest budgeting reuse depth explicitly in OPD.
  </details>

- **[RLVR$^{2}$: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23457)**  `arXiv:2609.23457`  
  _Hao Li, Zhengkun Zhang, Gangqiang Hu, Zhen Zhang, Yude Gao, Dai Dai, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is expanding from tasks with well-defined correctness signals, such as mathematics and code, toward multifaceted quality requirements specified by multi-dimensional rubrics. Since policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a scalar reward. This aggregation is often treated as score scaling, but it implicitly determines how quality dimensions trade off during training. The prevailing practice, normalizing each criterion and taking a linear combination, assumes that cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion compensate for failures on another; both assumptions are unreliable when criteria are semantically heterogeneous. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking (RLVR$^2$), a verifiable ranking paradigm for rubric-based RLVR. For each criterion, RLVR$^2$ converts rubric scores into criterion-specific within-group ordinal outcomes, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. By retaining only within-group ordering and discarding raw score magnitudes, RLVR$^2$ avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales. It further supports objective-preserving attribute adjustment: auxiliary attributes that correlate with observed rankings but are not training objectives can enter the estimation without expanding the rubric or rewarding them directly. Across three model scales and 16 benchmarks, RLVR$^2$ consistently outperforms representative rubric-based baselines, achieving the best overall performance on most benchmarks at every scale. Analysis shows it controls systematic effects tied to reasoning efficiency and response formatting while preserving the quality objective.
  </details>

- **[Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19956)**  `arXiv:2609.19956`  
  _Tung Tran, Viet Bao Mai, Hoang Ta, Tuan Dam_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.
  </details>

- **[Fairness Auditing After Model Updating: Reliability of Paired Disparity Comparisons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09788)**  `arXiv:2609.09788`  
  _Aaron Ceross, Tingting Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model updates can change disparities in prediction errors between demographic groups. We examine whether retrospective audits can reliably assess these changes by comparing updated models with their unchanged initial models on the same independent labelled observations, holding completed updating histories fixed. The target is the updated-minus-frozen difference in absolute subgroup gaps, averaged equally across reporting periods and assessed separately for true-positive and false-positive rates. Exploratory controlled simulations and repeated audits of fixed simulated histories assess coverage and decision correctness for nominal 95% intervals. Across the broader history panel, changing interval construction can raise or lower estimated coverage. In one subgroup-drift setting, 2,000 true-positive-rate audits evaluated twenty selected histories updated at fixed intervals, using 1,250 observations per reporting period. Replacing percentile bootstrap intervals with full-size basic intervals reduced estimated coverage from 92.20% to 84.55%. At an illustrative margin of 0.5 percentage points, correct conclusive decisions increased from 78 to 376, while incorrect decisions increased from 3 to 43, including 13 false reductions. The constructions used identical observations, estimates and bootstrap draws and had equal widths. Other controlled examples frequently excluded the population change while correctly indicating an increase. More conclusive audit results therefore need not provide more reliable evidence. Claims that updating reduced disparity require an inference procedure justified for the target and sampling design, an explicit decision margin, and group-specific performance reporting.
  </details>

- **[From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06912)**  `arXiv:2609.06912`  
  _He Zhao, Ryan Thompson, Daniel M. Steinberg, Ashfaqur Rahman, Edwin V. Bonilla, Cheng Soon Ong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. We then measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, although this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears once each model's average support is removed. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors, whereas its relationship to downstream model behavior mainly reflects differences between models and remains confounded with architecture and training.
  </details>

- **[CRAD: Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation for Decentralized Heterogeneous Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00446)**  `arXiv:2609.00446`  
  _Baraa Bilbeisi, Mengchen Fan, Baocheng Geng, Qing Tian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conventional federated learning (FL) relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: it demands an identical architecture and degrades under non-IID data. Real-world deployments usually break both assumptions. We sidestep both by building a decentralized knowledge distillation framework in which each client evaluates its peers' model snapshots on its own local data and distills from the resulting soft predictions. Because knowledge is transferred through the shared class posterior, clients are free to run different architectures; and because every teacher is evaluated on the student's own device, raw data never leaves the client, with no central server or public dataset required. Within this setting, we identify and address an under-examined problem: how to combine the peer teacher predictions. Existing methods, like uniform averaging, ignore how knowledge reliability varies across teachers and classes. We propose Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation (CRAD), which, per class, first discards teachers that disagree with the peer consensus and then takes a weighted average of the rest, weighting each teacher by its per-class reliability (precision, or inverse variance). Since the variance of an accuracy from $n$ samples scales as $1/n$, support enters automatically: among the teachers that survive filtering, a teacher is trusted for a class to the degree that it is both accurate and well-evidenced for it. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST, across heterogeneous architectures under severe non-IID skew, CRAD consistently outperforms competing methods in global accuracy. Our code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Does Latent Planning Survive Point Clouds? Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models for Geometric Observations and Goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29434)**  `arXiv:2608.29434`  
  _Fabio F. Oberweger, Michael Schwingshackl, Markus Murschitz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Latent action world models let agents plan new behaviors at test time by predicting how actions change the environment, and joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) do so by forecasting future latent states rather than pixels. Yet nearly all such models see the world through a camera, even though robotic manipulation is fundamentally geometric: in robotics goals for manipulation are traditionally specified by target object poses, not by images of the object once placed. We ask whether latent planning survives a shift from appearance to geometry, on the observation side as well as on the goal specifications side. To answer this, we extend the stable-worldmodel evaluation platform with simulated LiDAR-style raycast point clouds as a new sensor modality, and adapt three JEPA designs to point clouds: a frozen-encoder model built on Utonia features, a distribution-prior model based on LeWM, and an action-sensitive model based on Delta-JEPA. We further introduce a goal-encoding mechanism that constructs the goal latent from the current latent and a 3D target pose, removing the need for goal images or goal point clouds. A comparative evaluation of the different anti-collapse mechanisms shows that point-cloud world models can match their image-based counterparts, demonstrating that the modality shift from appearance to geometry is achievable. All models are released as open weights with open-source training and inference code, to make world-model planning accessible for LiDAR-driven and pose-directed robotic tasks.
  </details>

- **[CommitKV: Commit-Aligned KV Cache Compression for Multimodal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07855)**  `arXiv:2608.07855`  
  _Weizhong Huang, Jinchao Zhang, Xiawu Zheng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multimodal agents gather visual evidence through reasoning and tool use, extending their ability to solve tasks beyond the initial input. However, accumulating observations increases KV cache memory and inference costs. Token eviction reduces these costs by retaining useful cached tokens. Existing methods use attention, redundancy, or stage-specific queries to rank tokens, without explicitly comparing the same history across tool interactions. When observations shift attention, they may mistake temporarily reduced influence for lost usefulness and evict information needed later. We propose CommitKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that accounts for this changing evidence use. Commit-aligned measurement compares the deletion effects of the same page before a tool call completes and after its observation returns. Lifecycle-aware compression retires pages with low influence in both windows and temporarily protects pages influential before the call. Joint scoring combines attention importance, key redundancy, and token-level deletion effects to fill the remaining budget. Extensive experiments cover four open-weight multimodal models and eight benchmarks. CommitKV achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared compression methods on all four models. On Qwen3-VL-8B, it achieves 69.85% at a 512-token budget, only 0.91% below FullKV, and exceeds the strongest compression baseline by 8.44% at 256 tokens. Deploying the Qwen3-VL-8B agent with SGLang and vLLM at a 256-token budget reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 54.37%-55.23% and accelerates end-to-end inference by 2.12-2.17$\times$ over FullKV on the matched workload.
  </details>

- **[Glioma IDH Classification via CVAE: Synthetic Augmentation, Generative Classification, and MIL for Raman Biopsies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10196)**  `arXiv:2607.10196`  
  _Andrei Iuşan, Daria Voiculescu, Ion Petre, Andrei Păun, Bogdan Oancea, Mihaela Păun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Biomedical Raman datasets used in machine learning for glioma diagnostics are characterized by small cohort size and absence of diagnostic tissue annotations. We address both problems using a $\beta$-regularized conditional variational autoencoder and a dataset of 59 glioma biopsies from 46 patients for binary IDH-status classification. The $\beta$-CVAE was used as a: (1) Raman spectra generator; (2) generative classifier of Raman spectra; (3) Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) classifier of biopsy slides. Four classifiers were trained on real spectra, synthetic spectra, or a combined set and evaluated on held-out real slides. Random Forest and XGBoost achieved accuracy $0.83$ with synthetic training and $0.81$ with real training. Augmentation increased RF+SVM accuracy from $0.76$ to $0.83$; changes for the other classifiers were smaller. We show that the $\beta$-CVAE model can successfully be used in training IDH-status classifiers and as a generative classifier, with comparable results to other models; however, the results of using it in MIL are inconclusive and further study is needed.
  </details>

- **[A Few Teacher Steps Go a Long Way: Efficient SFT Data Collection for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04574)**  `arXiv:2607.04574`  
  _Junze Ye, Jiayi Cheng, Miao Lu, Michal Mankowski, Jose Blanchet, Mohsen Bayati_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  DAgger-style supervised finetuning (SFT) combines full teacher demonstrations with teacher continuations of partial student rollouts, providing supervision on contexts the student encounters. We study how to allocate the teacher-inference budget on these on-policy (OP) continuations after initial behavior cloning (BC). One existing collection recipe runs the teacher to termination and retains only successful continuations (OP-Success). Since rejected outputs still incur teacher-inference costs, we compare this recipe with shorter continuations without outcome filtering (OP-Short), and with continuing only failed learner rollouts while retaining successful continuations (OP-Critical). We evaluate these choices against acquiring additional full demonstrations, tracking total teacher-inference cost separately from retained training tokens. Across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and OpenThoughts-TB-Dev, teacher continuations improve the accuracy-cost tradeoff over scaling full demonstrations. On HotpotQA and OpenThoughts-TB-Dev, OP-Short surpasses the strongest tested BC baseline while reducing estimated teacher-inference cost by 20% and 83%, respectively, and on ALFWorld five-step continuations cut teacher tokens by 22% relative to full continuations with little accuracy loss. Controlled HotpotQA ablations show that by focusing on failed student rollouts, OP-Critical achieves comparable accuracy to OP-Success with 30% lower estimated teacher-inference cost and 36% fewer retained training tokens. Compute-matched comparisons with reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation further support brief teacher continuations as an efficient and lightweight post-training recipe.
  </details>

- **[Same Concept, Different Directions: Cross-Modal Feature Heterogeneity in Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29888)**  `arXiv:2606.29888`  
  _Chungpa Lee, Jihoon Kwon, Kyle Min, Jy-yong Sohn_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models map images and text into a joint embedding space. However, these embeddings often entangle multiple semantic features, which limits their interpretability and controllability. While sparse autoencoders have emerged as a useful tool for decomposing these embeddings into monosemantic features, their application to joint embedding spaces has largely relied on an implicit, untested assumption that semantically corresponding features share the same directions across modalities. In this paper, we challenge this assumption by characterizing discrepancies in feature directions for the same concept across image and text modalities, a phenomenon we term cross-modal feature heterogeneity. We demonstrate that this heterogeneity is a key driver of the modality split, where a shared concept activates different latents depending on the modality. This finding further reveals why aligning latent activations alone is insufficient to resolve the underlying feature mismatch. Motivated by this observation, we propose an approach that trains modality-specific sparse autoencoders to preserve each modality's feature geometry, and then aligns corresponding features post hoc. Our method improves reconstruction fidelity and enhances performance in cross-modal retrieval and concept-conditioned retrieval.
  </details>

- **[RecallRisk-BERT: Joint Prediction of Severity and Reported Root Cause in FDA Medical Device Recall Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27174)**  `arXiv:2606.27174`  
  _Ali Semih Atalay, Sevgi Yigit-Sert_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Background and objectives: Recall severity and reported root cause provide complementary information for reviewing medical device recalls, yet previous studies have modeled them separately. We examined whether these two outcomes could be classified jointly using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records from openFDA. Methods: RecallRisk-BERT combines a fine-tuned PubMedBERT encoder for recall narratives with embeddings of product code, regulation number, and medical specialty to predict recall severity (Classes I-III) and reported root cause (nine consolidated categories). We evaluated all models on a stratified random split, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals for selected comparisons, and three models on a chronological split. Results: Under the random split, LightGBM achieved the highest severity macro-F1 (0.856), as well as the highest root-cause macro-F1 (0.798). RecallRisk-BERT's severity macro-F1 (0.852) did not differ significantly from LightGBM's and exceeded that of single-task PubMedBERT (0.806), whereas its root-cause macro-F1 was lower (0.710 vs. 0.726). RecallRisk-BERT also identified more Class I records than LightGBM (89.9% vs. 84.3%; %difference, 5.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 3.9-7.3). Observed and model-derived mean severity scores ranked the nine root-cause categories similarly. On later records, all three models scored lower; single-task PubMedBERT achieved the highest chronological macro-F1 for severity (0.494) and root cause (0.292), followed by RecallRisk-BERT (0.458; 0.278) and LightGBM (0.358; 0.184). Conclusions: Fine-tuned text-tabular transformer models scored higher than gradient boosting on later recall records, whereas joint learning improved severity only under the random split. Evaluation on reports as first submitted is needed before using these models for post-report triage.
  </details>

- **[MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27358)**  `arXiv:2605.27358`  
  _Yanbei Chen, Hanxian Huang, Ernie Chang, Jacob Szwejbka, Digant Desai, Zechun Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the de facto architecture for hundred-billion-parameter language models, yet its advantages at sub-billion scales for on-device deployment remain largely unexplored. To close this gap, we present MobileMoE, a family of on-device MoE language models with sub-billion active parameters (0.3-0.9B active and 1.3-5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. We first formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes MoE architecture under mobile memory and compute constraints, identifying an on-device sweet spot - moderate sparsity with fine-grained and shared experts - that is simultaneously memory and compute-optimal. Building on the derived architectures, we train MobileMoE with a four-stage recipe covering pre-training, mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and quantization-aware training, all on open-source datasets. Across 14 benchmarks, MobileMoE matches or exceeds leading on-device dense LLMs with 2-4$\times$ fewer inference FLOPs, and matches or surpasses the state-of-the-art MoE OLMoE-1B-7B with up to 60% fewer parameters. To bridge the last mile to mobile deployment, we provide the first efficient MoE inference on commodity smartphones with comprehensive on-device profiling. At comparable INT4 weight memory, MobileMoE-S delivers $1.8$-$3.8\times$ faster prefill and $2.2$-$3.4\times$ faster decode than the dense baseline MobileLLM-Pro.
  </details>

- **[NPSolver: Neural Poisson Solver with Iterative Physics Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25786)**  `arXiv:2605.25786`  
  _Bocheng Zeng, Rui Zhang, Runze Mao, Mengtao Yan, Xuan Bai, Yang Liu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Efficiently solving Poisson equations on complex, irregular domains remains a fundamental challenge in scientific computing, as classical iterative solvers often suffer from prohibitive runtime due to ill-conditioned systems. While neural operators offer a fast alternative, they typically rely on large-scale labeled datasets or struggle with unstable training dynamics when using physics-informed residual losses. We propose \textsc{NPSolver}, a neural Poisson solver trained without solution labels via iterative physics supervision. Instead of relying on fully converged numerical solutions or raw PDE residuals, \textsc{NPSolver} utilizes a small number of preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) steps to refine its own predictions, providing a more stable and well-scaled training signal. Theoretical analysis confirms that this iterative supervision serves as a well-conditioned error proxy and that a stop-gradient design is essential for optimization stability. To better capture boundary-driven features under mixed boundary conditions, we further introduce the Boundary-Aware Transolver (\textsc{BA-Transolver}) architecture that explicitly separates interior and boundary tokenization. Extensive evaluations on 2D and 3D irregular geometries demonstrate that \textsc{NPSolver} outperforms both physics-informed and data-driven baselines. Furthermore, a downstream thermal control task highlights the model's capability for conducting efficient and reliable gradient-based boundary control. We will release our codes and data atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Flash PD-SSM: Memory-Optimized Structured Sparse State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19150)**  `arXiv:2605.19150`  
  _Aleksandar Terzić, Francesco Carzaniga, Nicolas Menet, Yannick Biehl, Michael Hersche, Thomas Hofmann, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  State-space models (SSMs) face a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and expressivity that is mainly dictated by the structure of the model's transition matrix. Unstructured transition matrices enable maximal expressivity, as measured by their ability to model finite-state automaton (FSA) transitions, but come at a prohibitively high compute and memory cost. In contrast, most structured transition matrix forms are highly efficient both in runtime and memory consumption, but suffer from limited expressivity. Building on recent work on structured sparse SSMs, we propose PD-SSM, a novel SSM that achieves comparable throughput to widely-used structured SSMs with significantly better expressivity guarantees. PD-SSM maintains a trainable set of structured sparse matrices, a single one of which is discretely selected at each time-step, enabling FSA expressiveness at the level of unstructured matrices while maintaining the efficiency required for training models at scale. First, we validate PD-SSM against a suite of alternative models on synthetic mechanistic and state-tracking tasks, finding that its theoretical expressivity is achieved in practice. Second, on multivariate time-series tasks involving sequences of length over 17,000, we find that PD-SSM defines a new state-of-the-art (SoTA) accuracy among competing SSM methods. Finally, we demonstrate that PD-SSM is an effective drop-in replacement for hybrid LLMs, yielding improvements both in natural language state-tracking and in common language modeling scenarios. Up to 3B parameters, its training speed matches that of widely used SSMs, with less memory than DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Seeking the Unfamiliar but Memorable: Conceptual Creativity as Meta-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16477)**  `arXiv:2605.16477`  
  _Mengye Ren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  What does it mean to create a new concept, rather than retrieve a familiar one? Repeatedly sampling a generative model at the same prompt produces variations with similar styles and typical content. We propose that creativity is the production of stimuli that are unfamiliar to an adaptive observer at first sight, but quickly learnable from a few exposures. We formalize this as a Creator-Appraiser pair: a Creator generates a candidate, an Appraiser adapts to it for a few inner-loop learning steps, and the Appraiser's improvement becomes the reward the Creator optimizes through. We instantiate the framework with diffusion as the Creator, an autoencoder Appraiser on MNIST, and a CLIP Appraiser with a low-rank adapter for natural images. With a frozen diffusion model and no additional language conditioning, the meta-learning gradient is enough to produce both stylistic variations and concept compositions beyond what the base model can generate on its own.
  </details>

- **[Quantile-Coupled Flow Matching for Distributional Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08515)**  `arXiv:2605.08515`  
  _Michael Groom, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Lars Kunze, James Wilson, Nick Hawes_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DRL) models the full return distribution, making it well-suited to uncertainty-aware and risk-sensitive decision-making. Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) critics are increasingly adopted in DRL, offering dense velocity supervision and a natural axis for scaling critic computation. Yet they carry a hidden metric mismatch: the distributional Bellman operator is a contraction in the Wasserstein distance, but CFM critics pair source and Bellman target samples arbitrarily, so their loss does not control the Wasserstein distance to the Bellman target. We show that this mismatch can be fixed with a single sorting operation. Our method, FlowIQN, sorts source and target samples within each mini-batch so that each source quantile is transported to its matching target quantile, approximating the monotone optimal transport coupling. We prove that this quantile coupling makes the CFM loss upper-bound, up to a constant, the squared 2-Wasserstein projection error. To our knowledge, this makes FlowIQN the first flow-matching critic whose training is an approximate Wasserstein projection of the Bellman target, and the guarantee extends to shortcut models for few-step inference. Empirically, the quantile coupling recovers multi-modal returns more accurately than an otherwise identical uncoupled flow with as few as two integration steps. FlowIQN improves substantially on the flow critic Value Flows in a fixed-policy diagnostic and is competitive on offline RL benchmarks across multiple policy extraction methods, identifying the coupling as a central design axis for flow-based critics. Code:this https URL
  </details>

- **[Crafting Reversible SFT Behaviors in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06632)**  `arXiv:2605.06632`  
  _Yuping Lin, Pengfei He, Yue Xing, Yingqian Cui, Jiayuan Ding, Subhabrata Mukherjee, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) induces new behaviors in large language models, yet imposes no structural constraint on how these behaviors are distributed within the model. Existing behavior interpretation methods, such as circuit attribution approaches, identify sparse subnetworks correlated with SFT-induced behaviors post-hoc. However, the fine-tuned model may still carry the behavior through other pathways, so such subnetworks offer no guaranteed handle for selectively controlling SFT-induced behaviors at inference time. We pursue a constructive alternative by asking: can an SFT-induced behavior be deliberately compressed into a sparse subnetwork, termed a *carrier*, that is sufficient for the behavior and, by construction, necessary for it, while remaining controllable at inference time without weight modification? We propose (a) **Loss-Constrained Dual Descent (LCDD)**, which constructs such carriers by jointly optimizing routing masks and model weights under an explicit utility budget, and (b) **SFT-Eraser**, a soft trigger prompt optimized via activation matching on extracted carrier channels, to revert the SFT-induced behavior toward the base model. Across safety, fixed-response, and style behaviors on four model families, LCDD yields sparse carriers that preserve target behaviors while enabling strong reversion when triggered by SFT-Eraser. Our ablation study shows that triggered LCDD models are consistently closer to the base model than identically triggered standard SFT models. The crafted structure is therefore what drives this reversion. These results establish training-time construction as a practical route to localizing and selectively suppressing SFT-induced behaviors in deployed models.
  </details>

- **[Sequential Strategic Classification with Multi-Stage Selective Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04202)**  `arXiv:2605.04202`  
  _Ziyuan Huang, Lina Alkarmi, Mingyan Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Strategic classification studies the problem where self-interested individuals or agents manipulate their response to obtain favorable decision outcomes made by classifiers, typically turning to dishonest actions when they are less costly than genuine efforts. Prior works have demonstrated a fundamental inability to get out of this conundrum by only focusing on the design of a classifier. We note that prior work also heavily focuses on either one-shot settings or repeated interaction with the same classifier. Real-world decision making is often multi-stage, involving a sequence of potentially different classifiers as an agent progresses. This paper introduces a sequential, stochastic, multi-stage model of strategic classification, by capturing how agents adapt their behavior, through improvement actions (enhancing both observable features and true attributes) and gaming actions (enhancing only observable features), over multiple levels of classification with increasing difficulty as well as reward. For each level, we adopt a selective classifier that can abstain from making a prediction at low confidence.
