Reversed and random edits indicate that the gains come from the intended behavior, and the approach works best when the failure situation is recognizable and a simple correction can address it.
  </details>

- **[FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31705)**  `arXiv:2611.31705`  
  _Jiaqi Yin, Baoyue Zhang, Jiyuan Zhang, Wenxuan Liu, Zhaofei Yu, Yue Deng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31694)**  `arXiv:2611.31694`  
  _Erik Derner_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. On a unanimous vote, the minimum-expected-loss rule reduces calibration to one loss-derived threshold, so for two of six model configurations a gate on the vote alone never executed a clear instruction, costing 0.49 per item on TRUST-NAV against CATWAY's 0.13 and 0.09; the fused estimate avoided this on every set.
  </details>

- **[Exteroceptive Sensor Faults in Autonomous Vehicles: A Cross-Modal Taxonomy and Fault Injection Toolkit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31667)**  `arXiv:2611.31667`  
  _Davide Possenti, Daniele Cianca, Stefano Arrigoni, Francesco Braghini_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autonomous vehicles rely on cameras, LiDAR, and radar to perceive their surroundings, yet these exteroceptive sensors can be degraded by hardware aging, environmental interference, miscalibration, embedded software errors, and combinations of these causes, with direct consequences for perception quality and safety. Existing surveys and benchmarks mostly address individual sensors, isolated conditions, or vehicle-level consequences, and no common vocabulary relates fault origins across the three modalities. This paper reviews the literature on exteroceptive sensor faults and proposes a cross-modal, origin-driven taxonomy that organizes them into five categories, namely hardware, environmental, calibration, software, and synergistic faults, mapping each entry to its physical or logical mechanism, observable manifestation, and affected subsystem, and relating the categories to the safety analyses of ISO 26262 and ISO 21448. To make the taxonomy operational, we release an open-source fault injection toolkit with 94 symptom-level routines (41 camera, 27 LiDAR, and 26 radar), four graded severity levels, reproducible burst scheduling, and per-frame labels recording the fault category, affected subsystem, and severity. Examples on the Boreas dataset illustrate how each category alters camera images, LiDAR point clouds, and radar scans. Together, the taxonomy and the toolkit provide a shared reference and a controlled testbed for studying sensor reliability, developing and benchmarking fault detection and diagnosis methods, and building fault-annotated datasets for the safety validation of perception systems. The toolkit is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Collision Rendering: GPU-Accelerated Trajectory Planning on Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields with Risk-Bounded Collision Checking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31658)**  `arXiv:2611.31658`  
  _Byoungkwon Yoon, Han Gyeom Lee, Hojun Lee, Yuseop Sim, Daniel Sungwoo Bae, Martin Byung-Guk Jun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although radiance fields provide detailed scene representations for robotics, they remain underexplored for trajectory planning, without a widely agreed-upon way to translate learned spatial primitives into reliable collision criteria. To bridge this gap, we introduce Collision Rendering, the first trajectory planning framework on sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR), which supports GPU-accelerated, risk-bounded collision checking and a differentiable collision cost. Our key insight is that the structured volumetric density of SVR allows its rendering pipeline to serve as a fast numerical approximator of collision probability. We approximate the robot with collision spheres and place a coinciding spherical camera at each sphere. Under a probabilistic collision model, we derive an upper bound on each sphere's maximum directional collision probability from the camera's rendering pipeline. Evaluating this bound on the GPU yields a modular collision checker that integrates with established sampling-based planners without an auxiliary geometric map or changes to the learned representation. We further compute a collision cost and its gradients from rendered opacities through the same pipeline, extending the framework to trajectory optimization. Experiments demonstrate millisecond collision checking time on a consumer-grade GPU and collision-free trajectories in all queries, outperforming other radiance field-based planners.
  </details>

- **[FabricBench: A Standardized Policy Benchmark for Bimanual Fabric Manipulation with a Contact-Driven Deformable Simulator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31577)**  `arXiv:2611.31577`  
  _Wenkang Hu, Haoran Wang, Liu Liu, Wenchao Huang, Yiji Chen, Mengao Zhao, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fabric manipulation challenges robot policies with changing geometry, self-occlusion, and contact, yet standardized evaluation remains focused on rigid objects. We introduce FabricBench, a benchmark for bimanual fabric manipulation with six tasks spanning garments, silk, and bags, 10,000 simulation-ready assets, and controlled tests of configuration and appearance generalization. Built on an open-source solver in Newton, our simulator enables stable bimanual grasping, holding, and release through contact forces, without artificial attachment. Redesigned cloth-rigid contact and bidirectional force coupling support interactions among robot arms, fabric, and free rigid objects, allowing a bag to support its contents and transmit their weight to the grippers. In a controlled grasp-hold-release evaluation, our solver succeeds in all 45 trials, compared with none for the tested baseline configurations. Evaluating six representative policies, including vision-language-action models and world action models, reveals substantial remaining challenges: the best policy achieves 77% average success, while no policy exceeds 36% on long-horizon T-shirt folding. Under the most deformed initial T-shirt configurations, success falls to 6-14% across policies, with larger drops than under the evaluated appearance shifts. Zero-shot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$ on a real robot largely preserves task difficulty ordering across six tasks (Spearman $\rho=0.94$). These results establish FabricBench as a reproducible testbed for measuring fabric-manipulation capabilities and exposing limitations in configuration generalization. The project website is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Hi3R-VLA: Grounding Semantics and Actions in 3D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31535)**  `arXiv:2611.31535`  
  _Shizhe Chen, Paul Pacaud, Cordelia Schmid_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate 3D geometry, how to effectively exploit it for precise and generalizable action prediction remains a central challenge. We introduce Hi3R-VLA, a 3D policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities - vision, language, and action - in explicit 3D geometry for robotic manipulation. Our model integrates spatially-aligned visual features and language conditioning into point cloud representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. It then anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D coordinate frame and uses 3D-RoPE enhanced action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine point features to model geometric relationships between action targets and observed points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of semantic fusion within 3D and spatial alignment between observations and actions. With fewer than 250M trainable parameters, Hi3R-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo and DexSuite across diverse manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm grippers to dexterous hands. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate its effectiveness in the physical world. The model, code and dataset are publicly released atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Embodied Neuro-symbolic AI: Making Robot Behavior Auditable, Safe, and Scalable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31488)**  `arXiv:2611.31488`  
  _Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Jonathan Francis, Alessandro Oltramari_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) end-to-end systems have driven major progress in robot learning, yet they still face persistent barriers to dependable real-world deployment. In practice, these models often exhibit brittle generalization under distribution shift (i.e., novel objects, layouts, lighting, or contact conditions), limited physical and causal reasoning, and inconsistent fine-grained motor control. Critically, many VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit what a robot must not do, making it difficult to provide assurance in safety-critical settings. These limitations constrain scalability, maintainability, and trust when robots move beyond controlled demonstrations. We propose Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: a deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints. By combining knowledge-guided perception, constraint-aware symbolic planning, and hybrid learning, Embodied NeSy AI enables robots to reason about their environment, adapt to new tasks, and provide auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements, thus supporting scalable, trustworthy robot deployment.
  </details>

- **[Learning from Human Corrections through Temporal Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31446)**  `arXiv:2611.31446`  
  _Anjiabei Wang, Tesca Fitzgerald_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When people intervene to correct a robot, they provide information not only through how they correct its behavior, but also through when they choose to intervene. Existing approaches to Learning from Corrections focus on comparing the new trajectory to the robot's originally intended behavior, thus underutilizing the context of the robot's behavior before the intervention. In this work, we investigate how both pre- and post-intervention behavior can be translated into preference pairs for learning value functions that approximate a human's latent reward. We construct post-intervention preferences by comparing corrected behavior with the behavior it replaces, and pre-intervention preferences from temporal relationships among states leading up to an intervention. We evaluate the learned value representations through two downstream tasks: goal inference and correction forecasting. Our results show that post-intervention preferences are particularly effective for goal inference, while pre-intervention preferences provide strong correction-forecasting performance. Combining both sources of information performs strongly across both tasks, even when generalizing to participants unseen during training. These findings demonstrate that both when and how humans correct provide complementary information for learning value representations from corrective interactions.
  </details>

- **[EvoMisty: Building, Optimizing, and Evolving Capabilities on a Social Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31341)**  `arXiv:2611.31341`  
  _Xiao Wang, Lu Dong, Ifeoma Nwogu, Srirangaraj Setlur, Venu Govindaraju_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Social robots face diverse and changing tasks in companionship and education. LLM-based methods can generate task programs, but they still rely on manually developed control interfaces and predefined capabilities. They also lack a general mechanism to optimize completed tasks based on user-specified metrics and reuse performance improvements acrossthis http URLpresent EvoMisty, a plugin-based framework that enables coding agents to build and continually improve robot capabilities. EvoMisty builds a control program from official documentation and verifies candidate capabilities on a physical robot. Verified capabilities are stored in an atomic capability library and combined with existing skills to solve tasks. After task completion, EvoMisty can collect execution data, measure user-specified metrics, and iteratively improve task programs. It then distills reusable skills from final solutions into a skill library for futurethis http URLevaluate EvoMisty on a physical Misty II robot using Claude Code and Codex. The two agents construct 109 and 107 verified atomic capabilities, respectively. Both complete all 28 AutoMisty benchmark tasks and seven additional tasks beyond AutoMisty's capabilities. Optimization improves all seven evaluated metrics across five tasks. For example, dialogue response latency decreases by 52% and 71%, respectively. Reusing skills from one optimized dialogue task reduces latency by 33% to 72% in three other dialogue tasks without further optimization. All code and experimental videos will be publicly released through the webpage:this https URL
  </details>

- **[WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31126)**  `arXiv:2611.31126`  
  _Zien Wang, Yuhao Pan, Yunfeng Fan, Nan Cheng, Xin Xia, Wenchao Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce WeaveVLA, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $\pi_{0.5}$, achieving over 98% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9% to 82.0% and from 85.7% to 87.8%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6% to 70.0% under standard conditions and from 33.3% to 53.3% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.
  </details>

- **[RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30555)**  `arXiv:2611.30555`  
  _Jiawei Guo, Yu Huang, Dijiang Dong, Yue Liu, Peiran Ren, Wei Shen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
  </details>

- **[ConsisX: Cross-View Consistency Thinking in 3D for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30308)**  `arXiv:2611.30308`  
  _Yunhe Zhang, Long Gao, Yuedong Fu, Gang He, Li Xu, Chang Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
  </details>

- **[OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30184)**  `arXiv:2611.30184`  
  _Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Liang Li, Zhaosong Li, Lifeng Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A new surface observation can extend an object map while contradicting an earlier object assignment. Treating both updates as a single merge can join unrelated objects; keeping all earlier assignments leaves fragmented objects unresolved. We present a revision module that makes these decisions separately. Historical merges require shared-mask evidence to outweigh separate-object explanations across views, including after removal of any one observation. New measured points are assigned through local competition among object seeds supported by image masks. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the method improves mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762. On four further spatial holdouts, AP rises from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision reaches 23.251. Controlled comparisons attribute the gains to protecting existing identities, consolidating selected fragments, and assigning new points locally. The results also show where conservative merge decisions suppress useful updates. A garage recording demonstrates the same revision module on LiDAR--inertial--visual mapping outputs.
  </details>

- **[Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30099)**  `arXiv:2611.30099`  
  _Sunjae Jeong, Geunhyeok Yu, Dowoon Lee, Hyoseok Hwang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
  </details>

- **[SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29912)**  `arXiv:2611.29912`  
  _Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability. Project Page:this https URL
  </details>

- **[SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29682)**  `arXiv:2611.29682`  
  _Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces SparQ4D, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, SparQ4D achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
  </details>

- **[BO-COMM: Bidirectional Optical System for Simultaneous Localization and Communication in Swarm Robotics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29044)**  `arXiv:2611.29044`  
  _Cheng Hu, Haotian Wu, Qi Lin, Manrui Zheng, Shigang Yue, Tao Zou, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Swarm robotics experiments need to track where robots are, know what state each robot is in, and feed environmental information back to them. Reporting states over a shared radio channel can suffer from contention as the number of robots grows, while static fiducial markers provide pose but cannot report changing states. We present BO-COMM, a bidirectional optical system that observes pose and state through one camera and returns environmental cues through light. Each Colias IV robot, fitted with a CEU-PLUS extension unit, carries a ring of 12 LEDs: a five-bit marker encodes heading, and the remaining seven bits display one of 52 state codes. An overhead camera locates robot centers by ring-based voting and decodes position, heading and state for all visible robots from a single frame. In the downstream direction, a projector renders spatial cues such as virtual pheromone fields, and an infrared channel delivers addressed commands. At 2048x1280 resolution, image-processing time increases only modestly from 2 to 30 robots. Path-following, color-reporting and multi-pheromone experiments show the system closing the loop between optical state reports and projected environmental feedback in a 2.50 x 1.56 m arena.
  </details>

- **[HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27181)**  `arXiv:2611.27181`  
  _Jinlin Gan, Mingzhe Li, Junsheng Zhang, Zhibo Zhou, Jiahan Geng, Yuhua Luo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.
  </details>

- **[LocoMuJoCo: A Comprehensive Imitation Learning Benchmark for Whole-Body Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26293)**  `arXiv:2611.26293`  
  _Firas Al-Hafez, Davide Tateo, Oleg Kaidanov, Aditya Bhatt, Artur Zelik, Zhengyi Luo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Agentic Scaling of Embodied Tasks in Simulation for Synthetic Data Collection and Policy Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26046)**  `arXiv:2611.26046`  
  _Kang Wang, Xiaolei Zhou, Xiaoyu Wu, Zhendong Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scaling embodied interaction data requires a broad collection of usable tasks, yet specifying and validating each task instance remains costly. We present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework that expands existing task collections under human intent. Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. A task-generation agent reuses interaction structure to construct supported variations and revises incompatible configurations using validation feedback. A task-execution agent uses the same bindings and geometric records to select robot-supported skills and check completion against the original task criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,450 task instances from 20,323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97 saved instances per elapsed hour, with 62.26% of construction attempts passing the configured physical checks. The execution agent completes approximately 38% of evaluated tasks, with successful cases spanning object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement. Diagnostic analysis identifies improvement priorities in construction reliability, action selection, task-robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results demonstrate task-collection expansion with measured construction productivity and concrete execution evidence, providing a foundation for subsequent interaction-data collection for embodied AI.
  </details>

- **[ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21258)**  `arXiv:2611.21258`  
  _Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. However, an initial action chunk may deviate from the correct plan implied by the predicted future, and the predicted future often fails to reflect how it relates to the specific action output, leaving the prediction-action coupling underexploited and making the action hard to correct before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, consistent with the gains from rethinking in these ablations.
  </details>

- **[Robot Demonstration Videos Should Include Transparency Disclosures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18982)**  `arXiv:2611.18982`  
  _Nozomi Nakajima_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper argues that the robotics and AI community should adopt disclosure standards for demonstration videos. As physical and financial constraints limit direct public access to embodied AI, public dissemination of progress in robotics is mainly through curated demonstration videos rather than direct experience with the technology. In a large-scale (N=9,341), pre-registered experiment across six countries, we find that the general public struggles to discern both the visual authenticity (e.g., distinguishing real footage from CGI) and behavioral authenticity (e.g., distinguishing autonomy from teleoperation) of robot demonstration videos. The omission of these details distorts public perception, leading people to overestimate the ability of robots to perform tasks and navigate real world environments. Using evidence from behavioral science, we design a disclosure intervention and demonstrate that the inclusion of clear disclosures in robot demonstration videos significantly improves discernment of visual and behavioral authenticity, as well as understanding robots' capabilities. We propose the adoption of disclosure standards for robot demonstration videos to accurately calibrate public expectations and promote transparency in robotics research.
  </details>

- **[Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: 1st Place Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11464)**  `arXiv:2611.11464`  
  _Ilia Larchenko_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $\pi_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on my held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds, and it won first place in the challenge, with 0.988 in the organisers' final evaluation on 1,000 unpublished seeds per task.
  </details>

- **[On Agentic Manipulation Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09892)**  `arXiv:2611.09892`  
  _Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Chen Chen, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. Seethis https URLfor code and videos.
  </details>

- **[Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34873)**  `arXiv:2610.34873`  
  _Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose a control barrier function (CBF) framework using split covariance intersection (SCI) to fuse neighbor ranges and generate covariance-derived uncertainty scales for mapping and control. Pairwise constraints incorporate inter-step relative displacement to establish continuous-time safe-set invariance across discrete control steps under stated containment, feasibility, and synchronization conditions. A hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. Sequential local quadratic programs using preceding-UAV commands complete a 14-UAV search in 221.1 s with 0.45 m root-mean-square localization error while satisfying all separation and reference bounds. Comparisons across search regions, swarm sizes, sampled robust CBF, localizability and formation targets, and model predictive control quantify speed-accuracy-margin trade-offs. Tests on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, a typical UAV onboard computer, verify sub-4 ms mean control cycles and sub-5 ms mean full per-UAV onboard cycles, while Gazebo quadrotor flights verify mission completion and constraint compliance under over-water multipath, beacon-UAV drift, wind turbulence, yaw errors, and communication faults.
  </details>

- **[RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26663)**  `arXiv:2610.26663`  
  _Shengbang Liu, Zhengye Du, Zhilong Wan, Honghao Su, Chenxiang Xia, Chang Ge, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback on execution quality and progress toward the task goal. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models and general-purpose multimodal models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Models trained to grade partial outcomes and individual task steps exhibit strong fine-grained grounding, while reasoning over observation histories supports tracking of accumulated task effects. Strong forward-progress and memory scores can nevertheless coexist with poor responses to task regression. Even models with strong grounding and progress estimates struggle to recognize effective recovery and to give consistent feedback within and across valid executions. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09718)**  `arXiv:2610.09718`  
  _Masatoshi Tateno, Takehiko Ohkawa, Yueh-Hua Wu, Hanlong Li, Tatsuya Matsushima, Yoichi Sato, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.
  </details>

- **[RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09696)**  `arXiv:2610.09696`  
  _Mimo Shirasaka, Takehiko Ohkawa, Takuya Okubo, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Kei Ota_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.
  </details>

- **[Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09566)**  `arXiv:2610.09566`  
  _Genki Shikada, Kazuki Osamura, Masaru Ide, Tetsuya Ogata, Kanata Suzuki_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped during training. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. We evaluate six tasks on a real bimanual manipulator, simulating intermittent vision loss by jointly masking all vision tokens with 10% probability per inference chunk. Baseline successes decrease from 14/30 under normal conditions to 2/30 under vision loss, whereas TMD maintains an aggregate count of 15/30. TMD also exhibits smaller changes in action commands when chunks generated under vision loss arrive. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.
  </details>

- **[Concurrent Semantic Search and Mission Execution for LTL Missions in Unknown Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39153)**  `arXiv:2609.39153`  
  _Fernando Salanova, David Morilla-Cabello, Cristian Mahulea Poleuca, Eduardo Montijano_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Planning complex missions in unknown environments requires robots to reason simultaneously about what they should do and what they still need to discover. Existing approaches for solving LTLf missions typically assume a known environment, or separate the exploration of the environment from the execution of the mission, while semantic exploration methods look for one target at a time and ignore the mission being executed.To fill this gap, our main contribution is an adaptive high-level planning method that interleaves a task-driven semantic search with the execution of the mission, advancing both in a non-myopic manner.Our method leverages two representations built online, a metric-semantic scene graph, built with a Vision Language Model (VLM), that provides the evidence needed to locate the objects the mission refers to, and the deterministic finite automaton (DFA) encoding the mission, that indicates which of them matter at each mission state. At every planning stage, our planner selects the waypoints that are most valuable for both the semantic search and the advancement of the mission, valuing them over the remaining mission stages in order to avoid blocking states. The selected waypoints are then ordered in a single high-level plan, which is recomputed as new information arrives.In photorealistic indoor environments over five mission types, our method completes more missions than the compared approaches while having to cover less of the environment, and it does so with shorter paths and complying with the restrictions imposed by the mission.
  </details>

- **[Robo-Harness K1: Harnessing Robot-Use Agents via Perception Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29389)**  `arXiv:2609.29389`  
  _Zexi Li, Yehang Zhang, Wenqian Li, Haojian Huang, Chenxu Wang, Chunyang Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) understand manipulation scenes and instructions, yet as robot-use agents they struggle to turn 2D observations into the 3D relations that motion requires. We introduce Robo-Harness K1, a robot-use agent harness built on perception as tools. K1 offers region grounding, calibrated depth and geometry, persistent visual anchors, and projected grasp candidates as callable tools. The VLM calls them to measure the scene, chooses its next motion from the results, and measures again after it acts. On LIBERO-PRO, K1 raises Gemini 3.7 Flash from 16.7% to 71.7% and GPT-6 Astra from 63.3% to 93.3%, with the largest gains on spatial tasks. Without fine-tuning, the Gemini agent transfers to three RoboSuite arms, dual-arm RoboTwin tasks, and mobile manipulation in RoboCasa. In real-world experiments on a Piper arm, K1 completes eight of nine concluded trials across three tasks. Agentic post-training further distills a frontier model's traces into a compact agent: trained on 107 successful episodes, Qwen3.5-9B reaches 44.2% on new initial states and 13.9% on held-out task conditions, versus 30.2% and 0.0% for OpenVLA trained on the same episodes. Mixed training on traces from four environments raises held-out accuracy from 11.1% to 27.8% and RoboSuite success from 28.3% to 50.0%.   </details>

- **[ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07838)**  `arXiv:2609.07838`  
  _Boliang Liu, Wint Yi Poe, Jingyun Di, Riccardo Trivisonno, Giuseppe Caire_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Connected robotics is an emerging 6G application where mobile robots follow natural-language instructions to manipulate physical objects. The Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enable this are too large to run on the robot; a common trend is to offload inference to the cloud. The wireless link, however, limits how much sensing data the edge can transmit per control step. Two recent lines address this constraint: semantic communication codecs compress sensor data but require channel-specific retraining, and VLA token pruners select tokens from image but ignore the channel. Our insight is that the dense semantic information contained in the language already indicates which visual tokens matter. We propose ComVLA, a framework that uses this language guidance to adapt the VLA token budget to the channel capacity. Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 pp in average task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. These results demonstrate that co-designing VLA inference and wireless communication is a practical direction for 6G-connected robotics.
  </details>

- **[FluentAct: Efficient Action Continuations for Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13924)**  `arXiv:2608.13924`  
  _Shuo Bao, Ming Shang, Yuchen Huang, Hongjin Niu, Han Yu, Yilong Qiu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Asynchronous vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate new action chunks while robots continue executing committed commands. Because the robot moves during inference, a chunk generated from an earlier observation can introduce abrupt command changes at handoff. To address this problem, we introduce FluentAct, a framework for efficient action continuation that improves command continuity at handoff. Instruction-aware history and retrieved memory provide task context, while a latent rollout of committed actions constructs the handoff context. An ordered Haar generator predicts pairwise averages and conditional differences with two forward evaluations of a shared action expert. During offline training, a frozen reference samples candidates under the same request and committed prefix. We rank these candidates by command continuity and train the policy with a reference-relative flow-energy objective. The trained policy generates continuations directly without online candidate ranking. FluentAct improves task completion over BehaviorVLA on CALVIN, RoboTwin 2.0 Hard, and six real-world manipulation tasks, achieving a CALVIN average sequence length of 4.52. On LIBERO, it achieves 99.1% success and reduces handoff command jump and trend mismatch by 21.3% and 20.7%, respectively, relative to the variant without preference training. In a separate timing study in unpaced LIBERO simulation on an RTX 4090, its median request-to-handoff latency is 153 ms, 32.5% lower than native $\pi_{0.5}$.
  </details>

- **[FastBridge: Closing the Model-Based Realization Gap in Safety Filters on 3D Gaussian Splatting for Fast Quadrotor Flight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01200)**  `arXiv:2607.01200`  
  _Dario Tscholl, Yashwanth Kumar Nakka, Brian Gunter_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Fast quadrotor flight requires safe obstacle avoidance under tight onboard compute limits. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides a continuous, geometry-aware scene representation for perception-driven navigation, existing 3DGS safety filters use reduced-order models such as single- and double-integrators that ignore actuator limits and assume commanded accelerations are realized instantaneously. Building on an analytic collision cone barrier for 3DGS, we introduce a nonlinear, actuator-aware safety filter enforced through the full quadrotor dynamics. We derive a high-relative-degree collision cone exponential CBF (ECBF) and a backup CBF whose forward-simulated backup policy provides a certified admissible fallback whenever the QP is infeasible under input constraints. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS safety filter, our approach reduces trajectory jerk by 47% and runs 2.25 times faster. We demonstrate the ECBF in simulation and validate the backup CBF on hardware for real-time navigation in cluttered, perception-derived environments.
  </details>

- **[Explore From Sketch: Accelerating UAV Exploration in Large-scale Environments with Prior Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11708)**  `arXiv:2606.11708`  
  _Tiancheng Lai, Yuman Gao, Xiangyu Li, Ruitian Pang, Xingpeng Wang, Siqi Shen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Autonomous exploration with UAVs in large-scale, topologically complex environments often suffers from low efficiency due to suboptimal scheduling and detours. Prior maps (e.g., construction drawings), although usually imprecise and flawed, are readily available in many scenarios and have the potential to provide global structural guidance. This paper presents a novel exploration framework that leverages sparse, unaligned, and even discrepant 2D prior maps for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. First, a robust 2D-3D point cloud registration pipeline is proposed to align LiDAR observations with prior maps. The registration pipeline combines a GeoContext descriptor for single-frame candidate retrieval, a multi-frame verification mechanism for coarse transformation estimation with outlier rejection, and a Scale-ICP algorithm for refinement. The registration module can handle map discrepancies and provide multiple hypotheses when geometric ambiguities arise. To effectively utilize the registration results for exploration planning, we further develop a hierarchical viewpoint planning strategy under localization uncertainties. The hierarchical strategy first spatially attaches local viewpoints to prior guidepoints and adopts a Monte Carlo Tree Search solver to determine their traversal sequence under each registration hypothesis. To mitigate registration uncertainty, a risk-aware selector evaluates prior sequences using confidence-weighted travel risk, and a fixed-endpoint traveling salesman problem is formulated to generate an efficient local coverage path under the selected prior guidance. Benchmark evaluations reveal up to 34.2% improvement in exploration efficiency and 37.9% reduction in flight distance compared to state-of-the-art methods, while extensive simulations and field experiments further demonstrate robustness to prior map incompleteness and deformations.
  </details>

- **[Integrated cooperative localization of heterogeneous measurement swarm: A unified adaptive method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04932)**  `arXiv:2603.04932`  
  _Kunrui Ze, Wei Wang, Guibin Sun, Jiaqi Yan, Kexin Liu, Jinhu Lü_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The cooperative localization (CL) problem in a heterogeneous measurement swarm with different measurement capabilities is investigated in this work. In practice, heterogeneous sensors lead to directed and sparse measurement topologies, whereas most existing CL approaches rely on multilateral localization with restrictive multi-neighbor geometric requirements. To overcome this limitation, we enable pairwise relative localization (RL) between neighboring robots using only mutual measurement and odometry information. A unified adaptive RL estimator is first developed to handle heterogeneous and unidirectional measurements. A distributed CL strategy is then developed in which each robot estimates its pose relative to the anchor by composing each pairwise RL estimate with the corresponding neighbor's pose estimate relative to the anchor. This guarantees CL under a weakly connected directed measurement topology, which is the least restrictive topological condition among existing results. The proposed method is independent of specific control tasks and is validated through a formation control application.
  </details>

- **[FAVLA: A Force-Adaptive Multi-Rate VLA Model for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23648)**  `arXiv:2602.23648`  
  _Yao Li, Peiyuan Tang, Wuyang Zhang, Haojie Ren, Chengyang Zhu, Yifan Duan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general robotic manipulation, but contact-rich tasks still require timely action refinement using force/torque feedback. Existing force-aware VLA models usually align all modalities to a single low operating frequency, which discards high-frequency contact cues that are important for reactive action correction. Additionally, they use static fusion, which cannot adaptively balance visual context and force feedback across manipulation processes. To mitigate these issues, we propose FAVLA, a force-adaptive multi-rate VLA model that explicitly separates low-frequency semantic reasoning from high-frequency force-conditioned action refinement. Specifically, FAVLA uses a low-rate VLM to encode visual-language-force context and predict near-future force statistics, while a high-rate action expert refines action chunks using the latest force observations. To decide when to update actions, we introduce a Force-Adaptive Multi-rate Inference (FAMI) mechanism, which schedules the action expert's inference rate from predicted future force variance, keeping low-rate reasoning in stable phases and increasing update frequency near contact transitions. To decide how to use force, we design a Force-Guided Dynamic Fusion (FGDF) module, which injects high-frequency force features into the action expert and dynamically balances visual-semantic and force cues across manipulation stages. Extensive real-robot experiments on high-precision and contact-rich tasks show that FAVLA outperforms force-aware VLA baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88.8% and lower peak contact forces. Zero-shot evaluations further demonstrate FAVLA's robustness to visual distribution shifts. Our project homepage is available at this website.
  </details>

- **[Learning Legged MPC with Smooth Neural Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12169)**  `arXiv:2601.12169`  
  _Samuel A. Moore, Easop Lee, Boyuan Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep learning and model predictive control (MPC) can play complementary roles in legged robotics. However, integrating learned models with online planning remains challenging. When dynamics are learned with neural networks, three key difficulties arise: (1) stiff transitions from contact events may be inherited from the data; (2) additional non-physical local nonsmoothness can occur; and (3) training datasets can induce non-Gaussian model errors due to rapid state changes. We address (1) and (2) by introducing the smooth neural surrogate, a neural network with tunable smoothness designed to provide informative predictions and derivatives for trajectory optimization through contact. To address (3), we train these models using a heavy-tailed likelihood that better matches the empirical error distributions observed in legged-robot dynamics. Together, these design choices substantially improve the reliability, scalability, and generalizability of learned legged MPC. Across zero-shot locomotion tasks of increasing difficulty, smooth neural surrogates with robust learning yield consistent reductions in cumulative cost on simple, well-conditioned behaviors (typically 10-50%), while providing substantially larger gains in regimes where standard neural dynamics often fail outright. In these regimes, smoothing enables reliable execution (from 0/5 to 5/5 success) and produces about 2-50x lower cumulative cost, reflecting orders-of-magnitude absolute improvements in robustness rather than incremental performance gains.
  </details>

- **[Follow-Bench: A Unified Motion Planning Benchmark for Socially-Aware Robot Person Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10796)**  `arXiv:2509.10796`  
  _Hanjing Ye, Weixi Situ, Jianwei Peng, Yu Zhan, Bingyi Xia, Kuanqi Cai, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Robot person following (RPF)---mobile robots that follow and assist a specific person---has emerging applications in personal assistance, security patrols, eldercare, and logistics. To be effective, such robots must follow the target while ensuring safety and comfort for both the target and surrounding people. In this work, we present the first comprehensive study of RPF, which (i) surveys representative scenarios, motion-planning methods, and evaluation metrics with a focus on safety and comfort; (ii) introduces Follow-Bench, a unified benchmark simulating diverse scenarios, including various target trajectory patterns, crowd dynamics, and environmental layouts; and (iii) re-implements eight representative RPF planners, ensuring that both safety and comfort are systematically considered. Extensive simulation experiments provide a quantitative study of safety- and comfort-related physical indicators, while real-world trials of two MPC-based implementations on a differential-drive robot illustrate deployment feasibility and practical following behaviors. These results reveal open challenges and future research directions.
  </details>

- **[Collision Risk Estimation via Loss Prediction in End-to-End Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07425)**  `arXiv:2503.07425`  
  _Ziliang Xiong, Shipeng Liu, Nathaniel Helgesen, Hongwei Li, Joakim Johnander, Per-Erik Forssen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Collision risk estimation and avoidance play central roles in the safety of autonomous driving (AD) systems. Recently emerged end-to-end AD systems gain collision avoidance ability by minimizing losses to penalize planning trajectories that are too close to other objects. Despite a significant collision rate during testing, most end-to-end planners do not explicitly quantify the collision risk in their outputs. To address this, we introduce RiskMonitor, an efficient plug-and-play module that interprets planning and motion tokens from state-of-the-art end-to-end planners to estimate collision risk. Inspired by loss prediction based uncertainty quantification, RiskMonitor predicts whether the collision loss -- commonly adopted to train end-to-end planners -- is positive along planned waypoints, framing collision risk estimation as a binary classification task. We evaluate RiskMonitor on the real-world nuScenes dataset (open-loop) and the neural-rendering based simulator, NeuroNCAP (closed-loop). Our token-driven method outperforms prediction-driven approaches, including deterministic rules, Gaussian mixture models, and Monte Carlo Dropout. When integrated with a simple braking policy, RiskMonitor improves collision avoidance ability by $66.5\%$ in a closed-loop test on safety-critical scenarios. These results demonstrate that monitoring collision risk using plan and motion tokens enhances the safety of end-to-end AD without retraining it.
  </details>
